Figure edited with contribution from Dr. Thais Baptista Teixeira.

sec.p: This position statement was prepared according to the new Brazilian Society of Cardiology guidelines, which call for objective, concise, and shorter documents, as well as the adoption of the format according to the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) system to indicate the level of evidence and strength of recommendations. This system consists of a simple grading model (strong, weak, or neutral recommendation; high, moderate, low, or very low certainty of evidence), as outlined in the diagram below.

Of note, diagnostic studies with adequate methodology that evaluate clinical outcomes are rare, even in the most prevalent cardiovascular diseases, such as CAD, heart failure (HF), and valvular heart disease. Hence, due to their low prevalence, randomized clinical trials, meta-analyses, and systematic reviews evaluating cardiac imaging methods for the diseases covered in this document are scarce or nonexistent. Thus, in some cases, even in the absence of large clinical trials, there may be a consensus that a particular imaging examination is clearly beneficial.

sec.title: 2. Applications of Multimodal Cardiac Imaging in Extracellular Matrix Disorders
2.1. Cardiac Amyloidosis
sec.p: Amyloidosis is a systemic disease that results in restrictive cardiac physiology due to the extracellular accumulation of amyloid protein fibrils in the myocardium, leading to ventricular stiffness, diastolic dysfunction and, eventually, HF. In addition to these morphofunctional changes, this progressive deposition is associated with significant electrical changes, such as atrial fibrillation and various atrioventricular blocks. It is important to highlight that there are 2 main subtypes of CA, which have distinct etiologies but very similar clinical manifestations.13,14

list-item.p: Light chain amyloidosis (AL), which results from the deposition of immunoglobulin light chains produced by a plasma cell disorder in the bone marrow.
Transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), which results from the accumulation of misfolded transthyretin, which can be wild-type (ie, without detected mutations), or hereditary due to genetic mutations.

sec.p: Differentiating between the AL and ATTR forms is challenging in clinical practice. However, the toxicity and quantity of fibril deposition is greater in AL than in ATTR, resulting in a more rapid increase in myocardial thickness,a higher incidence of pericardial effusion, and often greater impairment of systolic function parameters. Table 1 summarizes the main differences between these forms of CA.15–17

caption.title: Light chain amyloidosis vs. transthyretin amyloidosis

thead.style: border-top: thin solid; border-bottom: thin solid; border-color: #000000

tr.td: Excessive light chain production by plasma cells
Deposition of abnormal transthyretin (mutated or wild-type)
Primary (associated with plasma cell dyscrasias), or associated with multiple myeloma
Heart, kidneys, peripheral nervous system, gastrointestinal tract
Predominantly the cardiac and peripheral nervous systems
Middle age to older adulthood (generally > 50 years of age)
Older adults (> 60 years of age), especially wild-type
The presence of monoclonal light chains in serum and/or urine and amyloid infiltrate in tissue stained with Congo red dye
Genetic testing, scintigraphy with diphosphonates (99mTc-PYP, DPD or HMDP) and amyloid infiltrate unstained with Congo red
Chemotherapy, immunotherapy, autologous stem cell transplantation
Transthyretin stabilizers (tafamidis, diflunisal), RNA interference agents (patisiran and vutrisiran); emerging gene therapy

fn.p: 99mTc-PYP: 99m-technetium pyrophosphate; DPD: dicarboxypropane diphosphonic acid; HMDP: hydroxymethylene diphosphonic acid.

sec.p: Early diagnosis of CA depends on high clinical suspicion due to its initial non-specific presentation, like other cardiac conditions.18 Thus, increased ventricular thickness in patients without hypertension or aortic valve disease, associated with extracardiac signs, such as carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, peripheral neuropathy, or dysautonomia, can serve as an important diagnostic clue (Figure 1 and Table 2).19

caption.title: Spontaneous rupture of the biceps muscle tendon is a warning sign of suspected clinical amyloidosis, mainly the transthyretin form. A – Relaxed upper left arm with a portion of the biceps next to the ulnar fossa. B – Contracted left biceps muscle with no major changes in relation to relaxed muscles.
Warning signs of cardiac amyloidosis

thead.style: border-top: thin solid; border-bottom: thin solid; border-color: #000000

list-item.p: Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome
Family history of heart failure or neuropathy
Narrowing of the spinal canal with no obvious cause
Dysautonomia (mainly orthostatic hypotension)
Unexplained alterations in intestinal function
Spontaneous tendon rupture (generally the biceps tendon)
Low-voltage electrocardiogram, disproportionate to myocardial thickness
Pseudoinfarction pattern in electrocardiogram
Low-flow/low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction
Pacemaker (mainly with family history and increased ventricular thickness)
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
Unexplained proteinuria
Peripheral/autonomic neuropathy
Macroglossia (in light chain amyloidosis)
Ecchymoses, mainly periorbital purpura in light chain amyloidosis
Persistent elevation of troponin and natriuretic peptides in the brain
Edema syndrome
Unexplained weight loss
Presence of monoclonal paraprotein
Echocardiogram showing increased thickness with no obvious cause in the post-loading period
Reduced left ventricular longitudinal strain with an apical sparing pattern
Bone scintigraphy with intense cardiac uptake (Perugini grades 2 and 3)
In cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, diffuse late enhancement, elevated native T1 value and elevated extracellular volume

sec.title: 2.1.1. Echocardiography
sec.p: TTE is the first-line diagnostic imaging exam in CA.3 Based on the pathophysiology of the disease, in which progressive myocardial interstitial amyloidosis occurs, increased biventricular thickness may be observed, in addition to increased stiffness, and reduced ventricular compliance, with diastolic dysfunction, reduced stroke volume and reduced left ventricular (LV) GLS and an apical sparing pattern (Table 3, Figures 2 and 3).14,20–23

caption.title: Main echocardiographic findings in cardiac amyloidosis

thead.style: border-top: thin solid; border-bottom: thin solid; border-color: #000000

tr.td: Increased myocardial thickness with a concentric pattern, often symmetrical and significant (> 12 mm); a predominant increase with an asymmetrical pattern can be observed in the septal wall
Initially preserved left ventricular ejection fraction, progressing to systolic dysfunction in advanced stages
Restrictive diastolic dysfunction in advanced stages
Reduced global longitudinal strain with a typical apical sparing pattern
Thickening due to infiltration into the atrioventricular valves
Atrial dilation and dysfunction, which can affect both atria
Present in some cases, but with low sensitivity and specificity for diagnosis on its own
Progressive dysfunction is associated with poor prognosis; present in advanced stages
Present in advanced stages due to elevated left ventricular filling pressures

caption.title: Echocardiographic findings suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis. A – Parasternal long-axis view showing significantly increased ventricular thickness, reduced left ventricular diastolic diameter, and left atrial enlargement. B – Parametric image of reduced left ventricular global longitudinal strain (13.3%) with apical sparing.

Parametric analysis of left ventricle global longitudinal strain in a patient with light chain cardiac amyloidosis at 3 distinct time points: A – Initial diagnostic suspicion showing a reduced global value (13.6%) with apical sparing; B – 3 months later after diagnosis and the beginning of treatment; C – Follow-up treatment with chemotherapy, showing a significant drop in global longitudinal strain (8.9%) after 5 months, at which point the patient died.

sec.p: Multiparametric echocardiographic models have been developed to improve diagnostic accuracy.24 These models incorporate several echocardiographic parameters, such as relative wall thickness, E/e’ ratio, GLS, and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), to create more accurate diagnostic scores for CA.25

Echocardiographic assessment of treatment response in CA primarily involves analysis of functional and morphological changes in the myocardium. Key indicators of treatment response include reduced LV wall thickness and stabilization or improvement of GLS. The E/e’ ratio and left atrial (LA) stiffness are echocardiographic parameters that can reflect changes in diastolic function after treatment: improvement correlates with favorable treatment response.26–50

sec.title: 2.1.2. Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging
sec.p: CMR allows for precise evaluation of myocardial tissue changes associated with CA.27 Myofibril accumulation results in thickening of the LV walls and the interatrial septum, changes that can be detected by CMR morphological characterization and sequence analysis, often without significant dilation of the ventricular cavity.28,29 Increased atrial volume, diastolic dysfunction and, in advanced cases, reduced EF also occur.29 Pleural and pericardial effusions are common.29

As in the echocardiographic findings, patients with CA present with a more pronounced and diffuse reduction in GLS with relative apical sparing, in addition to reduced circumferential strain, especially in the basal regions.49 Biventricular strain analysis in CMR also allows detection of early right ventricular (RV) involvement, contributing to a more comprehensive assessment of the severity and extent of amyloid infiltration.50 CMR studies have found a significant correlation between LA dysfunction and amyloid burden, indicating that functional assessment of the atrial chamber can reveal early markers of cardiac involvement.51

Another observed tissue modification is increased total myocardial water content, which could result from volume expansion of the cardiovascular system due to the osmotic effect of accumulated proteins, as well as from increased intracellular water in myocytes subject to cytotoxic aggression from protein deposition, or even from reduced myocardial perfusion due to increased capillary spacing or obstruction.

The increased overall water content in myocardial tissue causes prolonged hydrogen relaxation times, both in the longitudinal (T1) and transverse (T2) axes.43 However, the most striking and clinically significant tissue alteration in CA is the marked expansion of myocardial ECV, which is attributed not only to the accumulation of amyloid fibrils during the symptomatic phases of the disease, but also to myocardial fibrosis repair. Therefore, the combination of protein deposition and interstitial fibrosis can be detected with high accuracy and even quantified through late enhancement (LE) techniques42,44 and myocardial ECV calculation.32–35 Normal myocardial ECV is around 25%, while in CA, especially the ATTR form, it can reach up to 60%.47,48

LE is one of the most common CMR techniques for CA assessment. A diffuse subendocardial or transmural enhancement pattern is typically observed, which contrasts with the more localized patterns seen in other cardiomyopathies.52,53 Global distribution of LE is associated with a higher amyloid burden and a worse prognosis.54 Typically, inversion of the myocardial recovery curve can be difficult to achieve, suggesting diffuse interstitial involvement.

Studies have shown that native T1 and ECV are significantly elevated in patients with amyloidosis, which can occur even in without visible LE, allowing for early diagnosis of cardiac involvement.52,55 ECV is highly sensitive to amyloid deposition. Recent meta-analyses have reinforced the role of LE, native T1, and ECV as predictors of mortality in cancer patients.55,56Figure 4 illustrates a case of CA evaluated by CMR.

caption.title: Cardiac MRI of a patient with cardiac amyloidosis. Cinematic MRI shows biatrial enlargement and increased biventricular myocardial thickness; late gadolinium enhancement images show diffuse involvement and elevated native T1 values and extracellular volume. ECV: extracellular volume; MRI: magnetic resonance imaging.

sec.p: Some initial studies have evaluated the role of CMR in myocardial strain assessment in patients with cancer, allowing for a more sensitive and earlier characterization of changes in myocardial function.49,50 Recent studies have demonstrated that, in addition to traditional GLS, parameters such as circumferential and radial LV strain, as well as RV strain components, offer further discrimination between AL and other conditions, such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.49

CMR could also play a role in therapeutic follow-up, indicating reduced ventricular mass.57 Serial quantification of ECV and native T1 could indicate a response to a specific therapy, such as transthyretin stabilizers or chemotherapy for AL.58,59 ECV reduction over time has been associated with clinical improvement and increased survival, highlighting its value as a marker of treatment response.55,59

CMR, together with findings from clinical history and laboratory data, allows differentiation of CA from other causes of increased myocardial wall thickness, such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or systemic arterial hypertension. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy usually presents with asymmetric thickening and localized enhancement, whereas pressure overload–related hypertrophy is generally not associated with changes in T1 or ECV. A diffuse LE pattern, a marked increase in ECV, and elevated native T1 values are characteristic of CA and help distinguish it from other forms of myocardial hypertrophy.29

sec.title: 2.1.3. Myocardial Scintigraphy
sec.p: Current Guidelines recommend initial investigation of CA using multimodal cardiac imaging. When CA is suspected, it is essential to exclude monoclonal gammopathy by measuring immunoglobulin-free light chains in blood and urine. Once gammopathy has been ruled out, 99mTc-pyrophosphate (PYP) scintigraphy becomes a highly accurate method. Myocardial tracer uptake with an intensity equal to or greater than that observed in the ribs (Perugini grades 2 or 3) allows the noninvasive diagnosis of transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis, without the need for endomyocardial biopsy. y (Figure 5).60

caption.title: Scintigraphy with 99m-technetium pyrophosphate showing more intense uptake than in the ribs (planar image, Perugini grade 3) and confirmed uptake in the myocardium in single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT). After monoclonal gammopathy was excluded, the patient was diagnosed with transthyretin amyloidosis. LV: left ventricular; RV: right ventricular.

sec.p: However, performing 99mTc-PYP scintigraphy requires adherence to specific technical criteria to ensure its diagnostic accuracy for transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis: (a) the need to confirm myocardial tracer uptake by performing tomographic scintigraphic imaging with single photon emission computed tomography, in order to avoid false-positive results due to radiotracer accumulation in the blood pool; and (b) careful exclusion of monoclonal gammopathy by means of serum and urine immunoelectrophoresis and assessment of blood light chains. Only after exclusion of light-chain involvement does technetium-99m pyrophosphate scintigraphy present adequate diagnostic specificity for the noninvasive diagnosis of transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis, without the need for biopsy, considering that up to 20% of light-chain cardiac amyloidosis cases may show tracer uptake on scintigraphy.

Patients with confirmed low-intensity myocardial uptake may present with early forms of the disease. In such cases, repeat imaging after 6 months is recommended when there is high clinical suspicion. In addition, some rare genetic forms, such as Ser177Tyr, Tyr114Cys, and Phe64Leu, may also present with disproportionately low 99mTc-PYP uptake, despite transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis with typical findings on echocardiography and CMR. In cases of high clinical suspicion with Perugini grade 0 or 1 technetium-99m pyrophosphate uptake (absence of uptake or uptake with intensity lower than that of the ribs), genetic sequencing is recommended to reduce the risk of diagnostic errors related to these rare mutations.61 Given the development of new treatments for alopecia areata, there is growing interest in determining whether imaging methods, including scintigraphy, can be used to monitor treatment response. However, this area is still under investigation, with the evidence in the early stages of consolidation.62

Observational studies have consistently demonstrated the applicability of scintigraphy in CA diagnosis and ATTR subtype identification63–66 (Table 4). The main limitations include a scarcity of large randomized clinical trials that have directly compared scintigraphy and biopsy regarding accuracy and prognostic outcomes, as well as the need for prognostic validation in different clinical contexts and populations. There is a clear recommendation that, when performed using an appropriate protocol, including the exclusion of monoclonal gammopathies, 99mTc-PYP scintigraphy may be sufficient to diagnose ATTR and that it has practical, ethical, and economic benefits over biopsy (Table 5).

sec.p: The recommended frequency of cardiac imaging examinations in patients with cardiac amyloidosis should be individualized according to the clinical status, the type of amyloidosis (AL or ATTR), response to treatment, and the availability of imaging modalities. According to current consensus statements, the following is recommended:

list-item.p: Echocardiography (including myocardial strain): every 6 to 12 months to monitor disease progression or response to treatment, and it may be performed earlier in cases of clinical deterioration or changes in biomarkers.[1–2] Myocardial strain should be included whenever available, as it is sensitive for detecting disease progression.

Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR): every 12 to 24 months, particularly in the presence of clinical worsening and suspicion of disease progression based on biomarkers or echocardiography, for detailed assessment of structural involvement or therapeutic response.58,60 There is no consensus supporting intervals shorter than 12 months in clinically stable patients.

Radionuclide scintigraphy (99mTc-PYP/DPD/HMDP): not recommended for serial monitoring of treatment response or disease progression, and should be reserved for initial diagnosis and definition of the amyloidosis subtype.58,60

caption.title: Key messages

list-item.p: In CA, multimodal cardiovascular imaging is imperative in clinical settings;
Echocardiography is the first-line cardiac imaging examination;
For echocardiographic phenotypes with increased thickness, GLS results demonstrating LV dysfunction and apical sparing, although not specific, increase the possibility of CA;
Even without signs of pulmonary hypertension (PH), RV function parameters may be reduced;
Despite advances, echocardiography cannot yet differentiate between AL and ATTR;

Clinical worsening is expected with increased ventricular thickness, atrial dilation, reduced LV stroke volume, worsening diastolic dysfunction, and a reduced GLS. Preserved EF may occur even in advanced stages;
In good treatment response, GLS will be stable or, in some cases, improve early, while morphological parameters change later;

CMR provides both morphofunctional evaluation and tissue characterization, quantifying the extent of myocardial involvement through LE, native T1, and ECV techniques. Diffuse LE and marked elevation of native T1 and ECV values are diagnostic and prognostic markers in CA;
99mTc-PYP scintigraphy, when performed using an appropriate protocol and after monoclonal gammopathies have been excluded, may be sufficient to diagnose ATTR, thus eliminating the need for biopsy.

sec.title: 2.2 Cardiac Sarcoidosis
sec.p: Sarcoidosis is a rare, multisystemic inflammatory disease with uncertain pathophysiology,67 characterized by the formation of non-caseating granulomas in different tissues. Its prevalence is around 230 cases per 100,000 inhabitants.68

Clinical manifestations range from asymptomatic cases to progressive and relapsing disease with significant sequelae.69 Intrathoracic involvement, which is quite frequent (97% of cases), is often due to intrathoracic lymphadenopathy (87%) or pulmonary parenchymal infiltration (50%), with respiratory symptoms described in 43% of patients.70 However, cutaneous, ophthalmological, renal, cardiac, and central nervous system manifestations, among other less frequent conditions, have also been described.71

Cardiac involvement is clinically diagnosed in approximately 3% of patients with sarcoidosis,72 although it is present in 27% to 69% of autopsied cases.73,74 The interventricular septum is the most commonly affected region, followed by the posterior wall, with significant LV involvement.75

The most frequent clinical manifestations are HF, atrioventricular block, and ventricular arrhythmias, present in 52%, 34%, and 24% of cases, respectively.76 In some cases, sudden cardiac death may be the first manifestation of the disease.77

Patients with CS frequently present with systemic involvement.72 However, in 18% of cases, cardiac involvement occurs in isolation and is associated with a higher incidence of sustained ventricular tachycardia and a greater chance of developing HF, probably due to later diagnosis.78

Although pulmonary disease remains the leading cause of sarcoidosis mortality worldwide, cardiac involvement is an important prognostic factor; it is the leading cause of death in Japanese cases.79 In treated patients, 10-year survival rates can reach 90%.80 Treatment with corticosteroid therapy is associated with lower mortality, symptomatic arrhythmias, and hospitalization for HF, as well as improved LV function.81 These data reinforce the importance of initiating immunosuppressive treatment during the inflammatory phase, before the development of potentially irreversible fibrotic lesions, which are associated with a worse prognosis. Hence, early diagnosis is fundamental.

Because myocardial involvement is not homogeneous, endomyocardial biopsy, despite having high specificity, has low sensitivity (< 25%).82–85 Furthermore, the inherent risks of the procedure cannot be disregarded, with complications reported in approximately 10% of cases.85 Due to improved multimodal cardiac imaging assessment and diagnostic criteria,86–88 which allow for diagnosis in the absence of a histopathological examination, routine endomyocardial biopsy is no longer justified.

sec.title: 2.2.1 Echocardiography
sec.p: In general, conventional TTE, despite wide availability and accessibility, has low sensitivity for diagnosing CS. However, when combined with 12-lead electrocardiogram and the patient's medical history, its sensitivity for diagnosing cardiac involvement is 64%.89 However, it remains the first-line test and, according to international guidelines, should be performed on all patients diagnosed with systemic sarcoidosis.87,90

A study conducted in India that evaluated patients with an established diagnosis of extracardiac sarcoidosis found that an absolute LV GLS < 17.3% had a sensitivity of 80%, a specificity of 82.61%, and a negative predictive value of 98.7% for diagnosing cardiac involvement, while an absolute RV GLS < 21% had a sensitivity of 68%, a specificity of 78%, and a negative predictive value of 98%.91

A recent meta-analysis of 478 patients with sarcoidosis found that LV GLS and TAPSE were significantly lower in patients with cardiac involvement, suggesting possible early diagnostic markers.92 Three meta-analyses have also found that patients with sarcoidosis without clinical manifestations suggestive of cardiac involvement have significantly lower LV GLS than healthy individuals.93–95 These findings suggest that changes in myocardial strain may precede structural or functional changes detected by conventional echocardiography, favoring early detection of subclinical myocardial dysfunction.

Figure 6 shows an example of myocardial strain assessed through speckle tracking in 2 patients diagnosed with sarcoidosis, with and without cardiac involvement, both with preserved LV ejection fraction (LVEF).

caption.title: Global longitudinal strain assessed through speckle tracking in 2 patients with sarcoidosis: (A) with cardiac involvement and (B) without cardiac involvement. In A, lower strain is observed in the basal segments of the septal walls and the lower and middle segments of the anterior lateral wall (lighter tones).

sec.p: In addition to significantly increasing diagnostic accuracy, myocardial strain also has prognostic implications. Reduced RV free wall strain has been associated with a higher incidence of ventricular fibrillation, sustained VT, advanced AV block, and hospitalization for HF.96 A correlation has also been found with late gadolinium enhancement in CMR and uptake in positron emission tomography with 18F- fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG positron emission tomography [PET]/CT).96 LV GLS has also shown increasing value in the prognostic assessment of patients with CS, being independently associated with a composite outcome of mortality, ventricular tachycardia, hospitalization for HF, and heart transplantation, in addition to being associated with uptake in 18F-FDG PET/CT.97

Some less sensitive, yet highly specific, findings that can affect prognosis should also be highlighted. LV dysfunction with LVEF < 40% is described in 21% of CS cases, while segmental abnormalities are found in up to 36% of patients,98 with possible progression to dyskinesia and aneurysms. Both have been associated with a higher incidence of all-cause mortality and severe ventricular arrhythmia,98 and they were included in the 2016 Japanese Circulation Society diagnostic criteria.88 However, only reduced LVEF was included in the 2014 diagnostic criteria.86,87Figure 7 shows transthoracic echocardiograms of CS patients with different patterns of LV dysfunction.

caption.title: Different patterns of left ventricular dysfunction in patients with cardiac sarcoidosis undergoing transthoracic echocardiography: apical 4-chamber view in diastole (A and C) and systole (B and D). In A and B, extensive involvement of the left ventricle is evident, with focal narrowing and significant dysfunction. In C and D, segmental dysfunction is evident, including the formation of an apical aneurysm and a thrombus (arrow) inside it.

sec.p: Narrowing of the basal segment of the interventricular septum (Figure 8), defined as thickness < 4 mm, is described in 28% of patients with CS.99 This has been considered an independent determinant of a composite outcome including all-cause mortality, symptomatic ventricular arrhythmia, bradyarrhythmia requiring pacemaker implantation, and admission for HF.99 It was also associated with LV dysfunction onset a median follow-up of 7.5 years.100

caption.title: Transthoracic echocardiography findings: narrowing of the basal segment of the interventricular septum (measuring 3 mm) in in the parasternal long-axis view during diastole (A) and systole (B).

sec.p: Ventricular involvement, which can occur primarily through granulomatous infiltration of the myocardium, has been described in 34% of cases76 (Figure 9). Secondarily, it can be caused by PH in association with primary lung involvement or advanced LV disease. In the absence of PH or diastolic dysfunction, echocardiographic findings of RV systolic dysfunction have a sensitivity of 10%-47% and a specificity of 82%-99% for diagnosing cardiac sarcoidosis.90

caption.title: Transthoracic echocardiography findings: right ventricular dysfunction in a patient with cardiac sarcoidosis, without pulmonary hypertension, likely due to primary involvement. Apical 4-chamber view focused on the right ventricle during diastole (A) and systole (B). In C, right ventricle global longitudinal myocardial strain (-14.9%) assessed through speckle tracking.

sec.p: Other less specific changes include diastolic dysfunction, mitral regurgitation, and pericardial involvement (Figure 10). Due to chronic inflammation in the myocardium, there is increased LV stiffness, with altered relaxation initially and increased filling pressures in more advanced cases.101 Minimal pericardial effusion has been described in 20% of patients with CS,102 but the disease can progress to constrictive pericarditis and cardiac tamponade.103

caption.title: Transthoracic echocardiography findings: less specific changes indicating cardiac involvement due to sarcoidosis. In A, B, C, and D, restrictive diastolic dysfunction is characterized (E/A ratio = 3.2, indexed left atrial volume of 39 mL/m², and E/e’ ratio = 16.9). A: Spectral Doppler of mitral inflow. B: Left atrial volume, assessed by Simpson's method, in the 4-chamber apical view. C: Tissue Doppler of the medial mitral annulus. D: Tissue Doppler of the lateral mitral annulus. In E and F, mitral valve insufficiency is evident in the long-axis parasternal view. E: 2-dimensional mode showing coaptation failure associated with apical traction of the cusps and dilation of the mitral annulus. F: Color Doppler analysis showing significant mitral regurgitation jet. In G and H, a discreet, posteriorly located pericardial effusion (arrows) in the subcostal 4-chamber view (G) and parasternal long-axis (H) views.

sec.p: However, mitral regurgitation is secondary in most cases, with the cusps exhibiting normal morphology and movement.104 Mitral regurgitation can occur due to mitral annulus dilation resulting from LA dilation associated with diastolic dysfunction, but it can also due to apical traction secondary to LV dysfunction. Recently, uptake in the papillary muscles has been demonstrated in 78% of cases with moderate or severe mitral regurgitation that were evaluated by 18F-FDG PET/CT, with 37% of patients showing a reduction of ≥ 1 severity grade after immunosuppressive treatment.104

sec.title: 2.2.2. Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging
sec.p: CMR is a noninvasive and highly sensitive method for assessing CS, providing anatomical, functional, and tissue data. Although morphofunctional assessment with cinematic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may be normal in the early stages, myocardial thickening, areas of regional hypokinesia and, in advanced cases, ventricular dilation and dysfunction can be progressively visible.105 Cinematic MRI can also identify ventricular aneurysms, pericardial effusions, and heart valve abnormalities – findings that may be present in individuals with CS.106

Classic CMR findings include LE in non-ischemic patterns. LE in basal segments of the lateral and septal walls, especially in mesocardial or subepicardial patterns, is considered the most frequent manifestation of CS.107 However, LE has also been identified in other areas of the myocardium, potentially involving the subendocardium and a transmural pattern.105,106,108,109 The LE technique has detected focal lesions in 20%–30% of patients with a biopsy-confirmed diagnosis, which were consistent with non-caseating granulomas.73,109 The extent of LE is related to structural cardiac changes, including reduced EF, LV dilation, and the occurrence of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia – factors already recognized as risk indicators for sudden cardiac death106 (Figure 11).

caption.title: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging of a patient with cardiac sarcoidosis. A and B: Cinematic magnetic resonance imaging showing a slight increase in myocardial thickness. C: Dark-blood images in triple inversion recovery with anterior hypersignal suggestive of edema. D, E, and F: Native T1 mapping sequences (D and E) and extracellular volume (F) with increased values. G, H, and I: Late gadolinium enhancement images showing multifocal fibrosis with different patterns (transmural, mesocardial, and epicardial) in different segments of the left ventricle.

sec.p: Advancement in multiparametric mapping, especially T1, T2, and ECV, has significantly improved the diagnostic accuracy and monitoring of inflammatory activity in sarcoidosis.105,110 T2-weighted imaging is sensitive to the presence of myocardial edema, which indicates active inflammation. In CS, elevated T2 values are associated with the acute phase of the disease, characterized by active granulomas and cellular infiltration (Figure 11). Focal or diffuse increases in T2 values can occur even without radiotherapy, making it a potential early marker of inflammation before fibrosis develops.111

In CS, elevated ECV values indicate both inflammation and chronic fibrosis, and their combination with T1 and T2 maps can distinguish different stages of the disease.112 ECV measurement proves particularly useful in longitudinal follow-up, enabling immunosuppressive therapy response assessment and the identification of disease progression, even without evident morphological changes73 (Figure 11). The combination of T1, T2, and ECV values can help identify different stages of CS:

list-item.p: Elevated T2 with normal T1/ECV: acute inflammatory phase.
Elevated T1/ECV with normal T2: chronic fibrosis without active inflammation.
All values elevated: concurrent inflammation and fibrosis, suggesting active, more advanced disease.

sec.p: This integrated approach to classic CMR findings (cinematic MRI and LE) with the use of multiparametric maps, is a useful tool for both early diagnosis and prognostic evaluation, as well as for therapeutic monitoring, being particularly beneficial in patients with nonspecific symptoms or inconclusive complementary examinations.110,111,113,114

sec.title: 2.2.3. Role of 18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography
sec.p: The 18F-FDG PET technique revolutionized CS assessment through in vivo identification of active inflammation in the myocardium, which is not possible with purely morphological examinations. This method is recommended by specialists for diagnosis and the monitoring and adjustment of immunosuppressive therapy.115,116

Recommendations on diagnosis and monitoring: 18F-FDG PET/CT is recommended for patients with suspected CS, especially those with atrioventricular blocks, ventricular arrhythmias, or ventricular dysfunction of undetermined etiology.115–118 Immunosuppressive treatment response should also be monitored every 3 to 6 months according to the clinical picture.115,116,119,120

Prognostic significance – right ventricular involvement: Because patients with RV 18F-FDG uptake have a significantly higher risk of adverse events, including arrhythmias and sudden death,121,122 early recognition is critical.

It is important to emphasize that sarcoidosis is a systemic disease and can affect multiple organs. Through whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT, extracardiac involvement can be identified, which contributes to both diagnostic confirmation and therapeutic choice.123,124 However, preparation for the test is crucial, as its accuracy depends on adequate preparation to suppress physiological uptake of glucose in the myocardium. Recommendations include:115,116,125,126

list-item.p: A diet high in fat and low in carbohydrates in the 24-72 hours before the exam;
≥ 12-hour fasting;
Beta-hydroxybutyrate ensures greater metabolic specificity (≥ 0.335 mmol/L predicts adequate suppression).127,128

sec.p: A 2020 meta-analysis of 17 studies (891 patients) found that cardiac perfusion and metabolism assessment had a sensitivity of 84% and a specificity of 83% in relation to these findings on the clinical spectrum of CS.117 Combined perfusion and metabolism assessment with 18F-FDG PET/CT distinguishes active inflammation (high FDG uptake) from fibrotic areas (perfusion defect without uptake), allowing for more precise stratification and individualized therapy (Figure 12).116–118 When available, combining it with CMR further increases diagnostic accuracy (Table 6).129

caption.title: 18F-FDG PET/CT in a patient with suspected cardiac sarcoidosis. (A) Axial slice demonstrating focal and heterogeneous 18F-FDG uptake in the left ventricular myocardium, predominantly in the interventricular septum, with extension to the right ventricular wall, consistent with active inflammation. (B) Coronal reconstruction showing the extent of myocardial uptake. (C) Sagittal reconstruction confirming the focal pattern of myocardial hypermetabolism.
Recommendations on multimodal cardiac imaging in cardiac sarcoidosis

sec.p: The recommended frequency of cardiac imaging examinations in patients with cardiac sarcoidosis should be individualized according to disease activity, symptoms, response to treatment, and risk of events. There is no international consensus on fixed intervals; however, major societies recommend echocardiographic evaluation (including strain analysis) every 6–12 months, annual cardiac magnetic resonance or at the clinician's discretion, and FDG-PET every 6–12 months in cases of active disease or during therapeutic adjustment.130–133

caption.title: Key messages

list-item.p: To increase diagnostic accuracy and improve prognostic assessment, myocardial strain assessment with speckle-tracking TTE is recommended for all patients diagnosed with systemic sarcoidosis. In patients with abnormal myocardial strain, further investigation with advanced imaging methods is recommended.

Although they are later findings, cardiac sarcoidosis dysfunction and segmental contractility abnormalities are included in the diagnostic criteria and are associated with a higher incidence of all-cause mortality and serious ventricular arrhythmias.

In patients with suspected cardiac sarcoidosis, it is advisable to look for thinning of the basal portion of the interventricular septum, defined as thickness < 4 mm in the long-axis parasternal view, as a prognostic marker.

18F-FDG PET/CT is essential for the diagnosis and monitoring of patients with suspected or confirmed cardiac sarcoidosis,115,116 particularly cases involving unexplained atrioventricular block, frequent ventricular arrhythmia, or unexplained ventricular dysfunction. 18F-FDG PET/CT also allows for systemic disease assessment.58,61,65,134

18F-FDG PET/CT has a prognostic impact, especially when for RV involvement.121,122 The patient must be properly prepared to avoid physiological myocardial uptake and ensure accurate interpretation of the results.125–128 This method allows for treatment adjustments according to inflammatory response.119,134
Combining 18F-FDG PET/CT with CMR improves differentiation between active inflammation and fibrosis.129

sec.title: 3. Applications of Multimodal Cardiac Imaging in Metabolic Diseases
3.1. Diabetes Mellitus
sec.p: Diabetes mellitus (DM), one of the most prevalent chronic diseases worldwide, significantly contributes to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.135 Myocardial impairment in individuals with DM, particularly type 2 DM (T2DM), can result from frequently associated comorbidities, such as CAD and systemic arterial hypertension. However, pathophysiological mechanisms specific to DM can directly affect myocardial structure and function.136 Glycemic alterations, such as insulin resistance and glucose metabolism dysfunction, promote systemic effects and directly affect cardiomyocytes, compromising energy substrate use, mitochondrial function, and excitation-contraction coupling.137 In this context, diabetic cardiomyopathy refers to cardiac dysfunction observed in patients with DM in the absence of other cardiovascular diseases, such as CAD, hypertension, valve disease, or congenital heart disease.137,138

Echocardiography plays an important role in diabetic cardiomyopathy assessment, identifying the 3 types of myocardial involvement: LV systolic dysfunction, diastolic dysfunction, and altered LV geometry. It can also help predict cardiovascular outcomes.135–138

Although reduced LVEF is considered to confirm HF137 in patients with suggestive symptoms, almost half of patients with HF and T2DM present with HFpEF, which is more frequent in older adults, hypertensive patients, and women with T2DM. HFpEF is usually associated with less severe complications in the early stages of T2DM, while HF with reduced EF is associated with more severe complications of T2DM, which suggests that the severity and duration of hyperglycemia are important factors in the development of LV dysfunction.139

Myocardial strain analysis with two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) speckle tracking has been used to detect subclinical systolic dysfunction in diabetic patients. Studies have shown that patients with DM present reduced LV GLS values, indicating systolic dysfunction even in the absence of evident clinical symptoms.135,140 In this context, reduced LV GLS is a sensitive marker of systolic dysfunction, detecting functional impairment even with preserved EF, and it is associated with the occurrence of HF, mortality, and LV remodeling.141,142

LV diastolic dysfunction is present in ≥ 50% of asymptomatic and apparently healthy patients with DM.137 Grade 1 diastolic dysfunction (ie, without elevated filling pressures) is weakly associated with prognosis. However, greater LV diastolic dysfunction, including increased LV filling pressure (estimated by the ratio of E/e′ wave velocities), is associated with adverse outcomes, such as progression to HF and mortality, and is consistently higher in patients with T2DM than controls.143,144

Concentric LV remodeling, an early change in myocardial structure, is associated with subtle systolic dysfunction resulting from steatosis and alterations in the myocardial energy chain.145 Hypertrophy (ie, increased myocardial mass) is partially attributable to ECV, reflecting collagen deposition and fibrosis, factors that are associated with worse outcomes.146,147 Hyperinsulinemia, resulting from insulin resistance, can also induce myocyte hypertrophy when there is increased afterload.148

LV mass index and LA volume have been associated with an increased risk of overall and cardiovascular mortality in patients with T2DM. These structural parameters, along with indicators of diastolic function (E/A and E/e’ ratios), are important predictors of mortality, highlighting the prognostic value of echocardiography in this population.149 Furthermore, LV diastolic dysfunction is frequently associated with LA dilation. Atrial fibrillation, a complication of DM, is attributed to increased LV filling pressure and atrial distension, which, according to other evidence in the literature, suggests arteriopathy.150

The heterogeneity of patients with asymptomatic myocardial dysfunction and DM could have important implications for therapy. A recent analysis identified 3 patterns in this population: 1) a group with less compromised systolic and diastolic function (predominantly men) that is associated with favorable prognosis; 2) obese patients with hypertension and diastolic dysfunction (mostly women); and 3) a group with LV hypertrophy (LVH) and systolic dysfunction (mainly men). The latter groups have similar, less favorable, prognosis.151

CMR enables detection of early myocardial changes and atherosclerosis, being an accurate technique for evaluating cardiac function at rest and under stress. It is a useful method for analyzing macro-/microcirculation in patients with DM.152–156

The CE-MARC study directly compared the ability of CMR and scintigraphy to detect CAD, using coronary angiography as the gold standard, finding that CMR as superior to nuclear medicine.157 The details of CAD assessment through imaging methods will not be covered in this document.

Although LE is the technique of choice for detecting and quantifying myocardial fibrosis, its utility in assessing diffuse fibrosis is limited, as it depends on the difference in signal intensity between normal and scarred myocardium.158 To overcome this limitation, parametric imaging techniques, such as T1 mapping and ECV quantification, have been developed.

T1 mapping, both before (native) and after contrast infusion, enables quantitative assessment of T1 values in the myocardium, identifying the presence of diffuse and interstitial fibrosis, which cannot be detected by circulating biomarkers or LE.158 In conjunction with the pre-contrast map, the post-contrast T1 map is used to calculate ECV.
In patients with DM, those with more severe CVD have a higher risk of cardiovascular events.159

T2-weighted images can detect myocardial edema, which indicates an acute response to inflammation (myocarditis) or ischemia, allowing for precise quantification and monitoring over time.158 In T2-weighted images, the signal intensity of myocardial lesions is higher than skeletal muscle, although they are not specific enough to detect diabetic cardiomyopathy (Table 7).

caption.title: Recommendations on multimodality cardiac imaging in patients with diabetes mellitus

thead.style: border-top: thin solid; border-bottom: thin solid; border-color: #000000

tr.td: Transthoracic echocardiography should be performed as a first-line assessment for patients with suspected heart failure.137,138,144
Systolic function should be assessed in appropriate acoustic windows using left ventricular global longitudinal strain when subclinical dysfunction is suspected.135,140–143

caption.title: Key messages

list-item.p: Diabetic cardiomyopathy refers to cardiac dysfunction in patients with DM in the absence of other cardiovascular diseases, such as CAD, systemic hypertension, valve disease, or congenital disease.
HFpEF is the most common initial clinical presentation in DM, while HF with reduced EF is a later and more serious complication of DM.
Reduced LV GLS indicates subclinical systolic dysfunction, even with preserved EF, and is a sensitive marker of HF, mortality, and ventricular remodeling.
Progressive LV diastolic dysfunction with a consistently high E/e′ ratio is associated with worse outcomes.
Increased LV mass index and LA volume are predictors of mortality.
Early metabolic changes in myocytes can be detected by CMR. Direct CMR assessment of the myocardium can determine disease severity.160
Microvascular disease, present in DM, is quantifiable through CMR and PET scans, although the latter is more expensive, less available, and involves radiation.161

CMR allows for early detection of cardiac changes in patients with DM, providing early identification of HF etiology (microvascular disease, subendocardial/transmural fibrosis, inflammation, or infarction).
CMR can identify hidden myocardial infarctions in up to 28% of patients with DM.161

sec.title: 3.2. Obesity
sec.p: Obesity, which is highly prevalent, is an independent risk factor for several cardiovascular diseases.162 New approaches to classifying obesity have been developed, but they are beyond the scope of this document; further reading is recommended.163 Among the hemodynamic and structural changes associated with this condition are LVH, LA and LV dilation, diastolic dysfunction, and subclinical systolic dysfunction. In obese patients without sleep apnea, early RV changes have been reported to precede LV changes.164

This document presents practical and up-to-date recommendations on the use of echocardiography and CMR in obesity, which are based on the best available scientific evidence and are presented according to the GRADE system. A summary of the main recommendations can be found in Table 8.

caption.title: Echocardiography recommendations for obese patients

thead.style: border-top: thin solid; border-bottom: thin solid; border-color: #000000

tr.td: Perform transthoracic echocardiography as a first-line cardiovascular assessment in obese patients with symptoms or risk factors.162,165
Ultrasound contrast agents should be considered in obese patients with insufficient acoustic windows to optimize diagnostic accuracy.165,168
Transesophageal echocardiography is safe and encouraged for indicated obese patients.165
Stress echocardiography can be used in obese patients to assess coronary artery disease.168
Systolic function should be assessed through global longitudinal strain when subclinical dysfunction is suspected in good acoustic windows.171
In obese patients, cardiac chamber indexing should be according to height, rather than body surface area.173,174
Epicardial adipose tissue can be quantified by echocardiography as a marker of cardiovascular events. Values > 10 mm indicate high risk.175

The right ventricle should be routinely assessed in obese individuals, even in those without pulmonary arterial hypertension, given that these changes occur early, preceding the left ventricle.164,165

sec.p: TTE, which is widely available, safe, and affordable, is essential for noninvasive cardiovascular assessment in this patient population.165 However, this method involves technical limitations due to their often insufficient acoustic window, requiring ultrasound contrast agents or supplementation with other modalities, such as CMR.166 In addition to morphological and functional cardiac analysis, CMR allows for tissue characterization, being especially useful for early detection of subclinical changes associated with obesity. Furthermore, CMR provides excellent image quality and high diagnostic accuracy, even at a mean BMI of 50.3 (SD, 5.9) kg/m².167 For cases involving an insufficient acoustic window, transesophageal echocardiography is a valid alternative, since it reduces the risks associated with sedation, provided that head elevation and monitoring with capnography and oximetry are observed.166

Another effective method is pharmacological stress echocardiography, especially when CAD is suspected.168 The Stress Ultrasonography in Morbid Obesity (SUMO) study found that although 96% of 205 patients required ultrasound contrast agents for adequate segmental assessment, pharmacological stress echocardiography was safe and had a positive predictive value similar to non-obese individuals.167 CMR also plays a prognostic role in obese patients with CAD. The Stress CMR Perfusion Imaging in the United States (SPINS) study found that reversible perfusion deficit and LE are independent markers of mortality in obese patients.169 More recent results have confirmed these findings in patients with BMI > 40 kg/m².170

In obese patients with good acoustic windows, LV GLS allows for complementary analysis of LVEF to assess systolic and mechanical function.171 LV GLS can detect early subclinical dysfunction, contributing to early treatment for HF or as a diagnostic adjunct in HFpEF.165,171,172

The indexing of cardiac chamber sizes and volumes in obesity is controversial, especially for the LA. Indexing according to body surface may underestimate dilation. For greater accuracy, allometric indexing according to height is recommended. Evidence suggests that this metric outperforms isometric indexing by body surface.173,174 Suggested values with indexing possibilities are described in Table 9.173,174

fn.p: BS: body surface; LAV: left atrial volume.

sec.p: Epicardial adipose tissue thickness, which is rarely used in clinical practice, has a good correlation with CAD.175 Epicardial adipose tissue is visualized as an echo-free space between the myocardium and the visceral pericardium. It is measured perpendicular to the RV free wall at end systole in longitudinal or transverse parasternal sections. Values > 10 mm are associated with higher cardiovascular risk.176

According to recent evidence, both bariatric surgery and semaglutide have a positive impact on cardiac structure and function in obese individuals due to weight loss and metabolic control, promoting significant regression of LV myocardial hypertrophy. Serial echocardiographic follow-up is recommended, which can show reduced LV mass, improved diastole, reduced LA mass, and increased GLS, without significant changes in LVEF.177–179 CMR is also recommended for monitoring structural changes following bariatric surgery.180

The performance of cardiac imaging examinations in patients with diabetes mellitus and obesity should be individualized, based on symptoms, cardiovascular risk, and clinical changes. There is no recommendation for routine cardiac imaging in asymptomatic patients solely due to the presence of diabetes or obesity, according to guidelines from the American Diabetes Association and the American Heart Association.133,182,183

Echocardiography (including myocardial strain) may be repeated according to clinical evolution, generally at intervals of 6 to 12 months in patients with established disease or persistent symptoms.133,183,184 In asymptomatic patients, echocardiography is not routinely recommended, but may be considered in high-risk cases or in the presence of biomarker abnormalities.137,185

Cardiac magnetic resonance and scintigraphy (including myocardial perfusion) are not recommended for periodic screening in asymptomatic patients with diabetes and obesity. These examinations are indicated in symptomatic patients for the evaluation of structural heart disease, or when echocardiography is inconclusive due to technical limitations related to excess adipose tissue.137,165,186 The frequency of imaging depends on the clinical indication, and there is no fixed interval recommended for follow-up in asymptomatic patients.

caption.title: Key messages

list-item.p: Ultrasound contrast agents are recommended to improve the diagnostic accuracy of TTE and pharmacological stress echocardiography in patients with insufficient acoustic windows, a condition frequently associated with obesity.165,168
LV GLS is superior to LVEF for detecting subclinical systolic dysfunction in obesity and should be performed whenever the acoustic window allows.171
In obese patients, allometric indexing of LA volumes by height is more accurate and should replace body surface indexing.173,174
Epicardial adipose tissue, which is measurable by echocardiography, can be monitored since it is associated with myocardial stiffness, diastolic dysfunction, and increased cardiovascular risk.175,176
High-quality CMR is possible regardless of the degree of obesity.
In obese patients, impaired perfusion and increased LE in CMR are predictors of mortality.
Cardiac ventricular mass and cardiac function are more accurately assessed through CMR, making it a suitable method for detecting early changes and assessing improvement after bariatric surgery.

sec.title: 4. Applications of Multimodal Cardiac Imaging in Rheumatological Diseases
4.1. Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
sec.p: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic, multisystemic, inflammatory autoimmune disease that frequently presents with cardiovascular manifestations, which are an important cause of morbidity and mortality in this patient population.
Pericardial disease, valve disease, PH, and myocarditis are the main cardiovascular manifestations in SLE, and echocardiography plays a role in their diagnosis and prognosis.1

Pericardial disease, the most common cardiovascular condition in SLE, is often its first manifestation and is present in up to 50% of cases. The vast majority of cases present with mild pericardial effusion, without major hemodynamic repercussions. Careful assessment of the clinical picture is essential to determine whether the presentation represents polyserositis or isolated pericardial effusion. In lupus pericarditis, which is frequently associated with a disease flare, patients may present with a characteristic clinical picture, including the classic triad of chest pain, fever, and pericardial friction rub, along with electrocardiographic changes and varying degrees of pericardial effusion. Complicated pericarditis is rare, and in only 1% to 2% of patients does the effusion become significant enough to result in cardiac tamponade. Constrictive or infectious pericarditis is rare.187

Valvular involvement in SLE is very frequent, reaching up to 75% in autopsy studies. Common lesions include nonspecific valvular thickening and Libman-Sacks endocarditis, which has a peculiar pathophysiology. These sterile verrucous lesions (deposits formed by immune complexes, fibrin, and platelet thrombus) are more common when SLE is accompanied by antiphospholipid antibodies. TTE aids in the differential diagnosis between Libman-Sacks endocarditis and infective endocarditis, an important consideration in immunocompromised patients. The mitral valve is more commonly affected in Libman-Sacks, and the lesions are generally located on its atrial surface and are less mobile. They can cause valvular disturbances (usually regurgitation) (Figure 13), embolic phenomena, and can serve as a substrate for infective endocarditis.188Figure 13 illustrates the case of a patient with a diagnosis of SLE presenting with aortic valvulitis and severe aortic regurgitation, as well as myocarditis, as assessed by echocardiography.

caption.title: Echocardiographic images of a patient diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus with aortic valvulitis and significant aortic regurgitation (A, B, and C), as well as myocarditis, which is evidenced by a reduction (-7.9%) in left ventricle global longitudinal strain in the 3-chamber view (D). In (A), transesophageal echocardiography shows moderate thickening and a slight retraction of the aortic valve opening (assessed in the long axis), associated with (B) significant regurgitation in color Doppler. In (C), continuous Doppler spectral curve shows a dense jet, associated with significant regurgitant volume and reduced pressure half-time (237 ms).

sec.p: The prevalence of PH among patients with SLE varies between studies, with estimates ranging from 0.5% to 17.5%. Typically, these are female patients of childbearing age and are classified as group I by the PH consensus.189 TTE is fundamental in estimating pulmonary artery systolic pressure, which is calculated using the maximum velocity of tricuspid regurgitation. TTE can also be used to assess direct and/or indirect signs of PH, such as a hypertrophied and dilated RV, an enlarged right atrium, a displaced LV (ie, lost sphericity, assuming a "D" shape), and a notch pattern in the RV outflow tract (suggesting high pulmonary vascular resistance). It is important to highlight that: 1) there is no specific pattern of PAH in SLE; 2) TTE allows for a probabilistic diagnosis, with right heart catheterization remaining the gold standard.190

The prevalence of myocarditis in SLE is still around 10%, despite significant advances in immunomodulatory drugs.191 In such cases, TTE plays a role in detecting segmental anomalies and determining the degree of systolic dysfunction (Figure 14). LVEF is sometimes preserved, but with GLS changes, frequently resulting in subclinical dysfunction.192 Additional factors can negatively affect myocardial function, as these patients often present with accelerated atherosclerosis and arrhythmias.

caption.title: Echocardiographic images of a patient diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus with significant ventricular dysfunction, evident in the apical 4-chamber view by the small variation in diastolic (A) and systolic (B) left ventricle diameters, with signs of spontaneous contrast in the left ventricular cavity. In (C) and (D), left ventricular ejection fraction (0.22) was calculated using Simpson's method; the apical 4-chamber view shows significant systolic dysfunction.

sec.p: In systemic diseases, recommendations for echocardiography depend on the prevalence of associated heart disease, the specific characteristics of cardiac involvement in each situation, and clinical suspicion of cardiac involvement.3

CMR has become the main noninvasive tool for early detection and tissue characterization of myocardial involvement in patients with SLE.193 Studies have found a high prevalence of myocardial fibrosis in these patients compared to controls, even in the absence of clinical symptoms. One of the largest cohorts involving CMR with LE found a significant frequency of myocardial fibrosis, which was often located in the inferolateral and septal regions and was associated with longer disease duration and the presence of multisystem involvement.194 Moreover, the location and extent of LE were associated with worse ventricular function and poorer clinical prognosis, suggesting its potential role as a prognostic marker.195

Quantitative techniques, such as T1 and T2 mapping, have also contributed to the assessment of inflammatory activity and tissue remodeling. Recent studies have shown that patients with SLE have elevated T1 and T2 values, particularly those who have not been treated with antimalarials.196 CMR with tissue tracking has also allowed subclinical biventricular dysfunction characterization in asymptomatic patients, helping identify those with increased cardiovascular risk who may benefit from early treatment.197

A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 studies (955 patients) comprehensively investigated the role of quantitative CMR biomarkers in patients with SLE, finding that individuals with SLE had significantly higher native T1, ECV, and T2 values than healthy controls. Furthermore, LV GLS was significantly lower in patients with SLE, suggesting myocardial inflammation and fibrosis, which was related to cardiovascular involvement and had prognostic implications.193

In addition to direct myocardial involvement, coronary microvascular dysfunction is a concern in patients with SLE, frequently associated with systemic inflammatory activity. A cohort study with a 5-year follow-up found that coronary microvascular dysfunction (assessed in perfusion-weighted MRI) and atherosclerotic plaques (assessed in CT angiography) were associated with future cardiovascular events, even in patients without significant coronary artery obstruction. These findings reinforce the importance of early screening for myocardial ischemia and vascular inflammation in patients with SLE.198

In addition, CMR has emerged as the most sensitive modality for diagnosing pericarditis in the autoimmune context, allowing the detection of pericardial thickening, effusion, and, above all, active inflammation through radiofrequency ablation and increased signals in T2-weighted sequences.194 A recent review on autoimmune pericarditis, highlighted CMR as essential not only for accurate diagnosis, but also for monitoring treatment response and detecting complications, such as transient or irreversible constrictive pericarditis.199 In patients with SLE, early identification of active pericardial involvement in CMR can directly affect therapeutic management, allowing for earlier immunosuppressive interventions and potentially preventing progression to chronic forms of pericardial fibrosis.

Therefore, CMR offers a comprehensive and sensitive assessment of cardiac involvement in patients with SLE, having potential not only for diagnosis but also for prognosis and therapeutic monitoring. Systematic incorporation of CMR in follow-up could result in the early detection of complications and better risk stratification for this patient population.

Additionally, nuclear medicine can contribute to assessment in the context of perimyocarditis and CAD.200 18F-FDG PET/CT has been used to assess acute pericarditis, confirming the presence of inflammation, demonstrating diffuse radiotracer uptake in the pericardium, generally at a low-to-moderate intensity. However, radiotracer activity in the pericardium is not specific, and cannot differentiate the etiology of different inflammatory or infectious processes, nor even neoplastic involvement.201,202 Because no studies have focused on 18F-FDG PET/CT in patients with SLE, this method should only be recommended as a complementary assessment in situations of diagnostic uncertainty.202

Similarly, 18F-FDG PET has been studied in relation to myocarditis in various clinical settings.203 In SLE, the evidence is limited to case reports, in which it aided diagnosis and treatment response assessment.204 Unfortunately, the procedure is expensive, not widely available, and involves radiation.

Patients with SLE have a high prevalence of CAD, and MPS may indicate myocardial ischemia, even without significant epicardial vessel obstruction or symptoms, which are associated with an increased occurrence of coronary events.205–207 Thus, MPS is useful for identifying myocardial ischemia and estimating cardiovascular risk in patients with SLE, which can be considered an equivalent of CAD.2 Myocardial perfusion studies using PET/CT with radiotracers (such as 13N-ammonia and 15O-H2O) have demonstrated changes in coronary flow reserve in patients with SLE, even without signs of systemic inflammation or cardiovascular symptoms, indicating the presence of persistent microvascular dysfunction in up to 57% of cases.208–210 Unfortunately, these radiopharmaceuticals are not produced in Brazil. Here, coronary flow reserve can be assessed through myocardial scintigraphy with a cadmium zinc telluride camera. However, no studies have used this method specifically in SLE (Table 10).

caption.title: Recommendations on cardiac imaging methods in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus

thead.style: border-top: thin solid; border-bottom: thin solid; border-color: #000000

tr.td: Transthoracic echocardiography should be performed in patients with SLE to investigate pericardial disease, valve dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, and myocarditis.1,187–190
Use cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with cinematic rendering, late enhancement, and T1/T2 mapping to assess cardiovascular involvement in patients with SLE.188
Use 18F-FDG PET to diagnose pericarditis and myocarditis.191
Use myocardial perfusion scintigraphy to detect myocardial ischemia.3,192,193

fn.p: 18F-FDG PET: 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography; SLE: systemic lupus erythematosus.

sec.p: Despite the wide range of cardiac manifestations in patients with SLE, there is still no standard routine for cardiac imaging screening in this population. However, the expert panel of this document recommends multimodal cardiac imaging evaluation for the early detection of cardiovascular abnormalities and risk stratification in this patient population, which carries a very high cardiovascular risk. The frequency of imaging examinations should be individualized based on clinical assessment of symptoms and disease activity, with annual echocardiography recommended in higher-risk patients.211–214

caption.title: Key messages

list-item.p: The main cardiac manifestations in SLE, in which TTE plays a diagnostic and a prognostic role, are pericardial disease, valve disease, pulmonary hypertension, and myocarditis.
Valvular involvement is quite common in SLE, and the most common type of lesion is nonspecific valve thickening.
The prevalence of PH in patients with SLE varies between studies, ranging from 0.5% to 17.5%. TTE is fundamental in estimating PA systolic pressure and assessing direct and/or indirect signs of PH.
TTE can provide a probable diagnosis of PH, with right heart catheterization remaining the gold standard.
In patients with SLE, myocardial involvement can be identified by CMR through the presence of non-ischemic pattern myocardial fibrosis and elevated native T1/ECV results.
Inflammation and edema can be adequately visualized in T2 mapping.
Pericarditis is relatively common in patients with SLE, with CMR being the method of choice for assessing active disease.

sec.title: 4.2. Systemic Sclerosis
sec.p: Systemic sclerosis is a rare autoimmune connective tissue disease whose pathogenesis is characterized by 3 markers: small vessel vasculopathy, autoantibody production, and fibroblast dysfunction leading to increased extracellular matrix deposition. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by serological tests and imaging studies.215 According to the American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism (ACR/EULAR), its main clinical features are skin thickening, Raynaud's phenomenon, and internal organ involvement.216 The type and severity of organ involvement will determine prognosis. Despite recent improvements in survival, systemic sclerosis has the highest morbidity and mortality of any rheumatological disease.215

Cardiovascular impairment is a major concern in systemic sclerosis, being one of the leading causes of mortality among these patients.217,218 Cardiac complications can be both primary and secondary, including arrhythmias,219 HF, pericardial disease, and myocardial fibrosis. Echocardiography is a widely available, noninvasive imaging method that plays a central role in assessing cardiac structure and function in systemic sclerosis. It is particularly useful for detecting both overt and subclinical cardiac involvement, as cardiac changes are often asymptomatic in the early stages of the disease. Because myocardial involvement is associated with a worse prognosis, it is important to identify early changes to prevent progression.

In patients with systemic sclerosis, TTE allows assessment of cardiac involvement, detecting systolic and diastolic dysfunction, valve abnormalities, and PH220 (Figure 15). Speckle-tracking echocardiography with myocardial strain assessment is especially useful for identifying subclinical myocardial dysfunction in patients with systemic sclerosis, which is often imperceptible through conventional echocardiography. Patients with systemic sclerosis present significantly lower myocardial strain parameters than healthy controls, indicating myocardial dysfunction involving the ventricles and the atria.221–226 Even when LVEF is preserved, GLS may be reduced in both ventricles,225 suggesting that this method may be more sensitive than traditional echocardiography in identifying early cardiac involvement.

caption.title: IEchocardiographic images of a patient diagnosed with systemic sclerosis and interstitial pneumonia. The images show normal systolic function (A) and increased left atrial volume associated with moderate diastolic dysfunction (B, C, and D). Right ventricle assessment shows preserved dimensions and systolic function through tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion and s’ (E, F, and G), but increased pulmonary systolic pressure (assessed with tricuspid regurgitation: flow velocity = 3.34 m/s) (H and I).

sec.p: Additionally, echocardiography is a valuable noninvasive method for initial assessment of pulmonary arterial pressure, especially considering that PH is associated with higher mortality in patients with systemic sclerosis.227 Pulmonary arterial pressure measurement by echocardiography can indicate the presence of interstitial lung disease, left heart involvement with increased pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, and pulmonary vasculopathy with associated PAH.227 However, although useful for PH screening, the diagnostic accuracy of echocardiography is considered moderate, with sensitivity and specificity around 83% and 72%, respectively.228 Due to its limitations, echocardiography should not be the sole measure for estimating pulmonary arterial pressure; it must be combined with other methods: right heart catheterization is considered the most reliable test for diagnosing and monitoring PH.228,229

RV monitoring is crucial for patients with systemic sclerosis and PH, as RV dysfunction is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Echocardiographic measurements, such as TAPSE, fractional area change, and tissue Doppler systolic velocity (S’) are routinely used to assess RV systolic function (Figure 15), together with 3D echocardiography and RV strain measurement.190 Additionally, inadequate RV adaptation to increased pulmonary arterial afterload is a determining factor in adverse outcomes in systemic sclerosis. Measurement of the RV-pulmonary arterial coupling, determined through noninvasive indices such as TAPSE/pulmonary artery systolic pressure and fractional area change/pulmonary artery systolic pressure, has prognostic value in identifying unfavorable clinical outcomes.230 It is important to highlight that the echocardiographic parameters used to assess ventricle function are limited due to the anatomical complexity of this chamber and the influence of loading conditions. Therefore, these parameters should not be used in isolation, but rather in conjunction with other indicators for more accurate assessment.190

Echocardiography can also detect asynchronous septal movement, which is related to the myocardial involvement observed in CMR. This echocardiographic finding antecedes abnormal MRI results, such as increased ECV and myocardial fibrosis, indicating cardiac involvement in systemic sclerosis.231

In addition to TTE, stress echocardiography can be used in systemic sclerosis, allowing detection of increased pulmonary artery systolic pressure229,232 and/or LV filling pressure233 during exercise, indicating HFpEF, which is associated with unfavorable clinical outcomes.232 PAH diagnosis should not be based solely on elevated pulmonary artery systolic pressure during exercise, since diastolic dysfunction, assessed by E/e’, is frequently observed in these patients.235 During stress echocardiography in patients with systemic sclerosis, it is crucial to monitor pulmonary artery systolic pressure, RV and LV function, and signs of pulmonary congestion. Complications, although rare, should be carefully monitored.

Finally, individualized management of systemic sclerosis, including cardiac complications, should be based on patient characteristics and disease severity, considering the extent of organ involvement. Treatment may include immunosuppressive therapy, vasodilators, and specific medications for cardiac complications (antiarrhythmics or HF protocols), as well as endothelin receptor antagonists or phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors for managing PH.235,236 Regular follow-up with TTE is essential to monitor treatment side effects, assess cardiac function, and optimize clinical outcomes.235

In patients with systemic sclerosis, CMR allows for detailed tissue characterization, enabling early detection of myocardial inflammation and fibrosis, which may be present even without clinical manifestations.

A non-ischemic LE pattern is a common CMR finding in patients with systemic sclerosis and indicates the presence of myocardial fibrosis, even in the absence of symptoms or evident ventricular dysfunction. LE is associated with a worse cardiovascular prognosis (arrhythmia and sudden death). In the multicenter Scleroderma Arrhythmia Clinical Utility Study (SAnCtUS), LE was an independent predictor of ventricular arrhythmia, reinforcing its prognostic value in this population.237 Advanced techniques, such as LE entropy analysis, have also shown additional prognostic value by quantifying the heterogeneity of fibrosis, which is associated with worse clinical outcomes.238

In addition to the LE technique, CMR allows assessment of diffuse fibrosis using native T1 maps and ECV. These parameters have been found to be elevated in patients with systemic sclerosis, even in early stages and without conventional changes, indicating subclinical myocardial involvement.239 T2-weighted imaging has also stood out in inflammatory activity assessment, being particularly useful in differentiating between active inflammation and chronic fibrosis. In a recent study, T2-weighted imaging demonstrated greater sensitivity than visual analysis in detecting myocardial inflammation associated with systemic sclerosis, even in asymptomatic patients.240

In another study that compared patients with systemic sclerosis to healthy controls, overall myocardial T1 and T2 values were significantly higher in patients with systemic sclerosis. Notably, 62% of patients with normal CMR findings (no LE or apparent edema) had elevated native T1 and/or T2 values. Moreover, 40% of patients with increased T1 values had larger LV diastolic volumes, larger biventricular systolic volumes, elevated global T2, and a more frequent history of digital ulcers.240

The emerging role of CMR in treatment response assessment is also important. In a prospective study, patients with myocarditis associated with systemic sclerosis were re-evaluated after immunosuppressive treatment, and a reduction in signs of myocardial inflammation was observed in T2 mapping and LE, demonstrating that CMR has potential in treatment response monitoring.242

A recent systematic review assessed the prognostic role of CMR in patients with systemic sclerosis. The main CMR parameters identified as consistent predictors of all-cause mortality were LE, native T1, ECV, and ventricular strain indices. Although less investigated, other markers, such as LA strain, perfusion measurements, and parameters obtained through stress CMR, have also demonstrated prognostic value but still lack robust validation.243

Evidence supports the use of nuclear medicine in cardiovascular evaluation of patients diagnosed with systemic sclerosis. Although limited to small clinical studies, the results are interesting. For more than 4 decades, MPS, first with thallium-201 chloride and later with 99mTc-sestamibi, has shown that approximately 80% of patients with systemic sclerosis have perfusion defects, even in the absence of atherosclerotic CAD. An association has been found between Raynaud's phenomenon and myocardial ischemia during pharmacological stress testing with dipyridamole or exposure to cold in approximately 50% of cases. These findings indicate that microvascular dysfunction and vasospasm are an important pathophysiological substrate for myocardial damage in this context.244–248

PET/CT coronary flow reserve assessment with 82rubidium has demonstrated that systemic sclerosis is an independent predictor of reduced flow reserve, which occurred in 89% of cases, being a marker of microvascular dysfunction in these patients.249

Diastolic dysfunction has also been observed in MPS with 99mTc-sestamibi gated SPECT imaging: those with a high total skin thickness score had a lower peak LV filling rate than those with a low score or the control group. This change was identified even in the absence of perfusion defects. The authors emphasized that this result might correlate with the severity of systemic sclerosis and, hence, it could serve as an early indicator of myocardial involvement. One study also found alterations in cardiac sympathetic function in 123I-MIBG scintigraphy, corroborating the hypothesis that autonomic dysfunction is common among in this patient population.250,251

Finally, abnormal myocardial radiotracer uptake in 18F-FDG PET/CT, an indication of subclinical myocarditis, has been observed in half of systemic sclerosis patients without cardiovascular symptoms, which may point to early cardiac involvement in the disease.252

More robust studies are needed to strengthen these findings and determine their prognostic impact. However, it seems reasonable to perform MPS to identify myocardial ischemia in patients with systemic sclerosis, especially symptomatic ones (Table 11).
