sec.p: Annual echocardiographic evaluation is recommended (including myocardial strain analysis, if available), cardiac magnetic resonance according to clinical indication every 2–3 years in high-risk or symptomatic patients, and myocardial scintigraphy only in selected cases.253–255

caption.title: Key messages

list-item.p: Cardiovascular impairment is common and is a leading cause of mortality in systemic sclerosis.
TTE is essential for assessing cardiac function and screening for PH.
Strain assessment with speckle-tracking echocardiography can detect early myocardial dysfunction, even with preserved EF.
RV assessment in patients with systemic sclerosis and PH is essential for therapeutic management and risk stratification.
Although TTE is important for PH screening, right heart catheterization is the gold standard for diagnosis.
Stress echocardiography can identify diastolic dysfunction, HFpEF, and PH.
Regular follow-up with echocardiography is important to guide treatment and monitor complications.
CMR can be used to detect cardiac involvement in patients with active systemic sclerosis.
In systemic sclerosis, morphofunctional assessment and tissue characterization with CMR is valuable for diagnosis and prognosis.

sec.title: 4.3. Ankylosing Spondylitis
sec.p: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic and progressive seronegative, inflammatory, and autoimmune spondyloarthropathy associated with human leukocyte antigen class I molecule B27. It is characterized by sacroiliac joint and spine involvement. The disease is also associated with enthesitis, uveitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and psoriasis.256–258

Patients with AS have a higher risk of cardiovascular diseases than the general population, including aortic and mitral valve insufficiency, aortic disease, HF, involvement of the conduction system, and CAD.257,259

Myocardial and valvular involvement is explained by the inflammatory and fibrotic process triggered by disease activity.257,259 Fibroblast activation and platelet aggregation have been demonstrated specifically in the aortic valve, resulting in valvular fibrosis.258
Table 12 shows the pathophysiology of cardiac and aortic involvement and its prevalence in individuals with AS.

Inflammation and fibrosis, with thickening and retraction of the valves.
Inflammation and fibrosis, with thickening of the mitral-aortic junction, resulting in reduced mobility or incomplete/asymmetrical coaptation of the cusps.
Inflammation and fibrosis, compromising left ventricle diastolic filling.
Extension of subaortic fibrosis, including involvement of the atrioventricular node, proximal His bundle and bundle branches and fascicles, resulting in conduction disturbances.

fn.p: ND: no data.

sec.p: Echocardiography is the imaging modality of choice for initial assessment and long-term follow-up of valvular heart disease. It is also the ideal tool for assessing diastolic function.3
Through LV GLS assessment, echocardiography can also show subclinical systolic dysfunction, revealing myocardial involvement, which may be present from the early stages of AS.259

In addition to evaluating ventricular function and heart valves, CMR can characterize myocardial tissue, demonstrating the presence of edema and/or fibrosis. In AS, myocardial edema can be observed, which is associated with disease activity, and focal LE, reflecting myocardial fibrosis.257 CMR can identify global LV dysfunction and focal areas of LE as definitive markers of cardiac involvement. ECV, quantified through myocardial T1 mapping, shows an association with the degree of disease activity, highlighting its potential as a biomarker for monitoring disease activity.257 Both CMR and CT can assess the aorta to detect dilation, stenosis, and signs of inflammation.
Although AS is associated with premature atherosclerosis and an increased risk of cardiovascular events, little has been published on the role of nuclear medicine in this scenario.

A study of 24 patients with AS concluded that, in young individuals, 18F-FDG PET/CT can show vascular wall inflammation and reduced inflammatory activity under the effect of statins.256 A study of 28 patients with AS used MPS with 99mTc-sestamibi, finding altered segmental motility through gated SPECT imaging in 8 patients, which is suggestive of microvascular dysfunction.257

Given the scarcity of evidence, no recommendations can be made regarding nuclear medicine methods specifically in the context of AS. However, this inflammatory disease shares pathophysiological factors with other systemic diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and SLE, in which MPS and 18F-FDG PET/CT have been used more extensively and have more established evidence and indications (Table 13).

sec.p: Currently, annual echocardiographic evaluation is recommended (including myocardial strain analysis, if available), cardiac magnetic resonance according to clinical indication every 2–3 years in high-risk or symptomatic patients, and myocardial scintigraphy only in selected cases. Cardiac imaging examinations in asymptomatic and clinically stable patients should not be performed at intervals shorter than one year, except in the presence of clinical findings.1,257,266–269

caption.title: Key messages

list-item.p: Patients with AS have a higher risk of cardiovascular diseases, including aortic and mitral valve insufficiency, aortic disease, HF, conduction system impairment, and CAD.
TTE is the method of choice for initial assessment and long-term follow-up of valvular heart disease and diastolic function.
LV GLS analysis may indicate subclinical systolic dysfunction, which can be present in the early stages of AS.
In addition to evaluating ventricular function and heart valves, CMR can characterize myocardial tissue, demonstrating the presence of edema and/or fibrosis.
Myocardial ECV is associated with the degree of disease activity, highlighting its potential as a biomarker for monitoring disease activity.
CMR and CT are the tests of choice for thoracic aorta assessment.

sec.title: 4.4. Rheumatoid Arthritis
sec.p: RA, an autoimmune, inflammatory, chronic disease with periods of remission and relapse, mainly affects the joints of the hands, wrists, feet, and knees. For reasons not yet fully understood, the immune system begins to attack the body's own tissues, especially the synovial membrane that lines the joints, causing pain, swelling, stiffness, and, over time, deformities and joint destruction. The disease can also affect other organs and systems such as the lungs (rheumatoid nodules and pulmonary fibrosis), the eyes (scleritis and keratoconjunctivitis), the skin, and blood vessels (vasculitis).265 In the heart, the main manifestations of acute RA are pericarditis, myocarditis, and endothelial injury, leading to increased cardiovascular risk.270

The diagnosis is clinical, based on signs and symptoms, supported by laboratory and imaging tests, including rheumatoid factor, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide autoantibody levels, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, radiography, and ultrasound for joint damage.. Although joint manifestations are the main clinical focus, cardiovascular complications, which often occur subclinically, are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in these patients.271
Thus, echocardiography is a fundamental diagnostic tool in the evaluation of patients with RA.

TTE allows for a noninvasive, safe, and effective assessment of cardiac structures and is indicated in patients with RA for detecting early changes such as diastolic dysfunction, pericardial thickening and effusions, valvular heart disease (especially aortic and mitral regurgitation), and alterations in ventricular contractility. Tissue Doppler echocardiography also contributes to a more sensitive assessment of myocardial function, even in the absence of evident clinical symptoms.272

Transesophageal echocardiography may also be indicated in more specific cases, when endocarditis or more detailed valve involvement is suspected, particularly in patients with new heart murmurs or unexplained embolisms. Thus, regular echocardiographic assessment can aid in the early diagnosis of cardiac complications, influence therapeutic management, and improve prognosis (Figure 16).273

caption.title: Transthoracic echocardiogram of a patient diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis, showing mild aortic valve thickening in the parasternal longitudinal (A) and transverse (B) views with mild regurgitation on color Doppler (C) and (D).

sec.p: In RA, several prognostic echocardiographic parameters have been identified, meaning they are associated with a higher risk of cardiovascular events, worse clinical outcomes, or mortality. These parameters allow for the diagnosis of subclinical cardiac involvement, facilitating earlier and more effective interventions.270

LVEF < 50% is associated with worse prognosis, but it is a late finding in most cases. Grade II or higher diastolic dysfunction, which is linked to an increased risk of HF and cardiovascular events, is prevalent even in early stages of acute RA, especially in women.

Patients with RA often present with reduced GLS, even when LVEF is preserved, indicating early myocardial damage, possibly related to chronic inflammation, fibrosis, or microangiopathy.274 Studies have shown a correlation between inflammatory marker levels (such as C-reactive protein and tumor necrosis factor-α) and GLS changes.275 This suggests that GLS may reflect the cardiovascular impact of inflammatory activity in RA, being useful both in baseline assessment and longitudinal monitoring. Reduced GLS in asymptomatic patients with RA could indicate a higher risk of future cardiovascular events, aiding in risk stratification and decisions about early intervention, such as intensified disease control or the use of cardioprotective agents. RV and atrial function, which can be affected by RA, can be assessed with GLS. This is particularly useful in cases with suspected pulmonary hypertension or chronic pericardial involvement.276

A meta-analysis demonstrated that increased myocardial mass is associated with progressive myocardial dysfunction and a higher risk of HF. In RA, it can occur even without hypertension, reflecting chronic inflammation.277

Another meta-analysis investigated case-control studies on valve and pericardial involvement in RA, finding that pericardial thickening or effusion is common in patients with long-standing RA, indicating chronic or acute pericarditis, even if asymptomatic. Persistent findings are associated with greater disease activity and the risk of complications, such as tamponade or constrictive pericarditis.278

Assessing pulmonary artery systolic pressure through tricuspid regurgitation velocity (> 35-40 mm Hg) also has prognostic value and is associated with increased mortality in RA, possibly reflecting advanced lung disease.272 Furthermore, RV dysfunction, whether assessed by traditional methods (TAPSE, s’, fractional area change) or RV GLS, is predictive of worse outcomes, especially in the presence of PH. A recent speckle-tracking study found that pulmonary ventriculo-arterial coupling can be used as a marker of early myocardial injury in RA.279

Three-dimensional echocardiography is a significant technological advancement in cardiac evaluation, offering real-time images with greater accuracy and anatomical detail than 2D echocardiography. In RA, this modality can provide specific benefits for both morphological and functional cardiac evaluation, especially regarding common subclinical cardiovascular manifestations in this patient population. Three-dimensional echocardiography provides realistic images of the valves, facilitating assessment of thickening, retraction, calcification, and functional changes.280

Several observational studies have also found increased cardiovascular risk in RA. A recent meta-analysis validated the use of carotid intima-media thickness as a marker of elevated cardiovascular risk in patients with RA.281 Carotid intima-media thickness is significantly higher in individuals with RA than healthy controls, reinforcing the role of vascular ultrasound, a widely available, low-cost method that allows early detection of plaques and thickening of the intima-media layer.2,211,212,282,283 Thus, vascular ultrasound is recommended as a screening method for subclinical carotid and femoral atherosclerosis.

Although echocardiography remains the initial examination of choice, cardiac CT and CMR broaden the assessment of cardiovascular involvement in acute RA, especially when greater anatomical precision, tissue characterization, or objective quantification of changes is needed, such as in subclinical cardiovascular disease, suspected myocarditis or fibrosis, early atherosclerotic risk assessment, and in cases where echocardiography is inconclusive. These examinations are particularly valuable in specialized centers and can contribute to more precise therapeutic decisions.284

Several studies have demonstrated the usefulness of CMR in early characterization of myocardial changes, even in patients newly diagnosed with RA and without a history of established cardiovascular disease. A recent study showed elevated T1 and ECV values in patients with active RA and the presence of autoantibodies, suggesting inflammation and early myocardial remodeling.285 Elevated T2 mapping values, suggestive of myocardial edema, are also found in patients with RA associated with disease activity.286 Furthermore, there is evidence that immunobiological treatment can positively affect the functional parameters of CMR LV assessment, reducing myocardial mass and improving LVEF.287–289

In addition to traditional risk factors, patients with RA have increased cardiovascular risk, partly due to chronic systemic inflammation. Cardiac CT, including coronary calcium score assessment and CT angiography, has proven an important tool in the early risk stratification and monitoring of subclinical atherosclerosis progression. A recent study demonstrated that patients with RA have significantly higher coronary calcium scores than healthy controls, highlighting the importance of cardiac CT in the early assessment of subclinical atherosclerosis.290 Furthermore, cardiac CT can also detect valve and artery calcification more frequently in these patients than in individuals without autoimmune diseases.291

The progression of coronary atherosclerosis in patients with RA also appears to be associated with the degree of cumulative inflammation, cardiovascular risk factors, and drug exposure. A prospective study using CT angiography found that patients with higher inflammatory activity and lower clinical control had greater atherosclerotic plaque progression, even after adjusting for traditional risk factors.292

However, therapeutic strategies aimed at rigorous inflammatory control have proven effective in reducing cardiovascular risk. Randomized clinical trials comparing immunomodulators have demonstrated that, in addition to controlling joint activity, they had a positive impact on vascular outcomes, such as reduced arterial inflammation and adequate control of the lipid profile.293,294 These effects can be monitored through noninvasive imaging methods, such as cardiac CT, and techniques associated with vascular inflammation detection, such as 18F-FDG-PET.

These findings highlight the relevance of CMR and cardiac CT as diagnostic and prognostic tools in patients with RA. They offer a detailed morphofunctional assessment and show potential in treatment response monitoring. The routine incorporation of CMR and cardiac CT into cardiovascular screening strategies in RA may allow for earlier and more individualized interventions.295

Nuclear medicine can contribute to the investigation of pericarditis and myocarditis in patients with RA, demonstrating the disease's inflammatory activity through 18F-FDG-PET/CT. The inflammation of large and medium-sized blood vessels and its relationship to cardiovascular risk has also been assessed with 18F-FDG PET/CT and PET/MR. Another application is myocardial ischemia assessment by myocardial perfusion scintigraphy or PET/CT using perfusion radiotracers.2

An interesting study found pathological uptake of 18F-FDG in the myocardium in 39% of individuals with RA. This finding correlated with clinical and laboratory criteria of disease activity, suggesting that the imaging method could be considered a marker of subclinical myocardial inflammation. The examination was repeated 6 months after treatment, showing a significant reduction in uptake in those who used tumor necrosis factor inhibitors, indicating adequate treatment response.296 It is important to mention that abnormal myocardial 18F-FDG results are not characteristic of any specific process; they only identify the presence of active inflammation. Definitive diagnosis depends on the integration of clinical, laboratory, and other imaging information, as well as the possibility of endomyocardial biopsy in selected cases, depending on the context.

Reports indicate that patients with active RA have increased 18F-FDG uptake in the carotid and aortic arteries, which is a sign of vascular inflammation. There is also evidence that RA treatment can reduce uptake intensity.297,298 However, it has also been shown that patients with chronic RA may continue to show signs of increased vascular inflammatory activity, even during remission.299,300

The most significant evidence regarding the impact of RA in the context of coronary artery disease demonstrated a reduction in coronary flow reserve on PET/CT with rubidium-82 or N-13-ammonia in patients with RA, which is similar to diabetics without a prior CAD diagnosis. In follow-up studies of up to 10 years, the mortality rate was higher in patients with altered coronary flow reserve. The results corroborate that RA, like diabetes, is a determinant of microvascular dysfunction and is associated with a higher risk of cardiovascular and all-cause mortality.301 However, these radiopharmaceuticals are not produced in Brazil. In our country, it is possible to assess coronary flow reserve through myocardial scintigraphy. However, no studies have specifically used this method in RA.

In all patients with RA, coronary risk should be assessed every 5 years or when changes occur in symptoms or anti-inflammatory therapy. Noninvasive tests to investigate myocardial ischemia and/or atherosclerosis may also be useful in this context (Table 14).2

sec.p: The frequency of cardiac imaging examinations in patients with RA should be guided by symptoms, clinical course, risk factors, and therapeutic changes, with no protocol for periodic screening in asymptomatic patients.2,211,212

caption.title: Key messages

list-item.p: The main cardiac manifestations of RA are pericarditis, myocarditis, and endothelial injury, leading to increased cardiovascular risk.
Reduced LVEF (< 50%) is associated with worse prognosis, but it is a late finding in most cases.
Grade II or higher diastolic dysfunction is linked to an increased risk of HF and cardiovascular events.
GLS is often reduced in patients with RA, even with preserved LVEF, indicating early myocardial damage.

Ventricular hypertrophy, or increased myocardial mass, is associated with progressive myocardial dysfunction and a higher risk of HF, and may occur even in the absence of arterial hypertension, reflecting chronic inflammation.

Nuclear medicine techniques, such as 18F-FDG-PET/CT, can be used in patients with RA to assess myocardial, aortic, and carotid vascular inflammation, as well as to detect myocardial ischemia using MPS.

Pericardial thickening or effusion is common in patients with long-standing acute RA, indicating chronic or acute pericarditis, and persistent findings are associated with increased disease activity and complications.
CMR morphofunctional assessment and tissue characterization are useful for detecting myocardial involvement, and the protocol should incorporate cinematic MRI, LE, and T1/T2 mapping techniques.
When indicated, atherosclerotic disease can be accurately investigated through coronary CT angiography and calcium score.

sec.title: 4.6. Takayasu's Arteritis
sec.p: Takayasu's arteritis (TA), a rare form of inflammatory vasculitis, was initially described in 1908. It preferentially affects large blood vessels, especially the aorta and its branches, and may also affect the coronary and pulmonary arteries to a lesser extent.302 Its incidence is higher in women and individuals < 40 years of age.303

The most common clinical manifestations in the initial phase of the disease include fever, arthralgia, myalgia, night sweats, loss of appetite, and weight loss. However, diagnosis usually occurs in more advanced stages, when vascular fibrosis is already observed, resulting in peripheral pulse changes and blood pressure differences > 10 mm Hg between limbs. At this stage, a murmur and thrill along the arteries may also be detected. In addition, the patient frequently presents with hypertension, which is one of the most common causes of diagnosis of this condition.304 Therefore, all young patients with hypertension of unknown cause should be investigated for TA.
The American College of Rheumatology diagnostic criteria305 are described below. Patients must present at least 3 of the 6 indicated parameters:

list-item.p: Age < 40 years.
Decreased brachial pulse.
Limping in the extremities.
Difference of 10 mm Hg in systolic blood pressure between the upper limbs.
Bruits over the aorta and subclavian arteries.
Angiographic changes in the aorta and its main arches.

sec.p: Comprehensive assessment with laboratory tests is recommended, especially markers of inflammatory activity (polymerase chain reaction and erythrocyte sedimentation rate), which can be useful in disease monitoring. Although diagnosis is based on clinical criteria, PET/CT has been used to assist to confirm diagnosis and monitor inflammatory activity, whether in treatment response assessment or in suspected inflammatory process relapse, especially when the symptoms are nonspecific and other tests are inconclusive.306,307

Therefore, in patients with TA, assessment of the entire aorta is recommended as early as possible by magnetic resonance imaging or computed tomography, with or without 18F-FDG, in order not to delay immunosuppression (level of evidence 1C).307–309 Tomography associated with 18F-FDG has high specificity in large cell arteritis and may be beneficial in patients with TA for determining inflammatory activity as well as the degree of vascular involvement (Figure 17).310 Activated inflammatory cells have an affinity for 18F-FDG, a glucose analogue used in PET/CT scanning, which can detect inflammatory and/or infectious diseases and is applicable in the context of TA.306,311

caption.title: Patient with suspected Takayasu arteritis, presenting paresthesia in the right upper limb during exertion. Doppler ultrasound of the upper limbs demonstrated right subclavian artery stenosis. A coronal PET image with 18F-FDG shows heterogeneous uptake of the radiotracer in the ascending aorta and carotid arteries, suggesting vasculitis.

sec.p: PET/CT has advantages over other imaging methods, including combining anatomical and functional images, estimating the intensity of the inflammatory process through the degree of radiotracer uptake, obtaining whole-body images in a single examination to identify the extent of the involvement, no impairment to renal function when the examination is performed without iodinated contrast media, and a low incidence of allergic reaction to the radiopharmaceutical. Potential disadvantages include high cost, low availability, and the use of ionizing radiation.312

A 2018 meta-analysis (10 studies; 301 patients) found a sensitivity of 81% and a specificity of 71% for identifying TA compared to clinical criteria.307 Another meta-analysis investigated the efficacy of PET/CT for monitoring treatment response in large vessel vasculitis, including giant cell arteritis (4 studies; 111 patients), finding a sensitivity of 77% and specificity of 71% for distinguishing active disease and remission.308 Some limitations that affect the diagnostic accuracy of PET/CT in TA are the small number of included patients, the diverse inclusion criteria, and the different image parameters analyzed in the studies.313–315

CT is less invasive than catheter arteriography and can clearly demonstrate thickening of the vessel wall, which may not be visible with catheterization316 (Figure 18). MRI can also be used to determine the degree of vessel wall involvement, with its main advantage over CT being the lack of ionizing radiation, which can be beneficial for monitoring young patients due to the need for frequent repeat assessments of the aorta.317 Both CT (with or without 18F-FDG) and MRI reveal lesions from inflammation due to the disease, a tortuous aorta, alternating segments of stenosis with dilation or occlusion, and aortic branch involvement, especially the carotid, left subclavian, and mesenteric arteries.318 Disease activity can be monitored through inflammatory function tests and imaging studies (MRI or CT angiography).

caption.title: Echocardiographic (A, B, and D) and thoracic aorta CT angiography (C) images of a patient diagnosed with Takayasu's arteritis. The patient presents with significant concentric myocardial hypertrophy (A and B) secondary to marked stenosis of the aortic arch, descending thoracic aorta, as well as occlusion of the brachiocephalic trunk and marked stenosis of the left common carotid artery and left subclavian artery (C). Continuous Doppler ultrasound showed a maximum gradient of 202 mm Hg in the suprasternal view of the descending aorta. Image provided by Dr. Viviane Hotta.

sec.p: Although using vascular ultrasound to assess thoracic aorta involvement in TA involves technical limitations, the method is important for detecting involvement of the subclavian arteries, common carotid arteries (sparing of the carotid branches), vertebral arteries, and abdominal branches (Figure 19). In addition to aiding in the diagnosis of atrial fibrillation, vascular ultrasound can monitor disease progression and treatment response.319 During periods of inflammatory activity, vascular ultrasound can visualize arterial segments with concentric thickening, which are characterized by homogeneity and low or intermediate echogenicity and may involve hypoechoic areas related to edema and/or neovascularization.320 In addition to neovascularization, artery diameter increases > 10 mm suggest disease activity.321 Concentric thickening can lead to arterial obstructions and occlusions, including ischemia in target organs. However, when vascular ultrasound detects arterial segments with hyperechoic concentric thickening due to a greater presence of fibrotic tissue, there is a stronger correlation with chronic stages of TA.319,322

caption.title: Stages of concentric thickening in Takayasu's arteritis. In a patient during the active phase of the disease, transverse (A) and longitudinal (B) B-mode sections demonstrating large concentric thickening of the common carotid artery wall with low echogenicity and echolucent intervals. Longitudinal B-mode sections demonstrating less pronounced and more echogenic thickening of the common carotid artery wall (C) with sparing of the internal branch (D). Image provided by Dr. Cláudia Maria Vilas Freire.

sec.p: It is recommended that:

list-item.p: Vascular ultrasound can be used to detect mural inflammation and/or luminal changes in the aortic branches of patients with suspected TA, but it has limited value for thoracic aorta assessment;

Vascular ultrasound can be used for long-term monitoring of structural damage, particularly to detect stenosis, occlusion, dilation, and/or aneurysms. Both the screening frequency and the imaging method should be decided on a case-by-case basis.

sec.p: Echocardiography, which plays a secondary role in clinical management, can be used to detect changes secondary to segmental stenosis of the aorta and its branches, arterial hypertension (ventricular hypertrophy) (Figure 18), and even the direct involvement of other vessels, such as the coronary arteries (up to 25% of patients may present with stenosis) and the pulmonary arteries, which may be dilated. Accelerated flow in the abdominal aorta (in the subxiphoid plane) and mitral or aortic valve insufficiency (which can occur in up to 55% of patients) may also be observed (Table 15).323

caption.title: Recommendations on the use of 18F-FDG PET/CT in Takayasu's arteritis

thead.style: border-top: thin solid; border-bottom: thin solid; border-color: #000000

tr.td: Use 18F-FDG PET/CT to diagnose active vascular inflammation and the intensity and extent of involvement.307–309
Use 18F-FDG PET/CT to monitor treatment response.307–309

fn.p: 18F-FDG PET/CT: 18F- fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography.

sec.p: Although not well established, the frequency of imaging examinations can vary from 3 to 6 months depending on disease activity and the clinical evaluation of individual patients.316 However, according to the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) recommendations, patients in remission should undergo vascular ultrasound, MRI, or CT annually, even in the absence of inflammatory activity after medication has been introduced, due to the possibility of subclinical vascular involvement.308

caption.title: Key messages

list-item.p: TA is a rare inflammatory vasculitis that frequently causes arterial hypertension and vascular fibrosis, resulting in bruits over the aorta and subclavian arteries, changes in peripheral pulses, and a blood pressure difference greater than 10 mm Hg between the limbs.
In patients with TA, evaluation of the entire aorta is recommended using MRI or CT, with or without 18F-FDG.
18F-FDG PET has high specificity for GCA and may be beneficial in patients with TA for determining inflammatory activity as well as the degree of vascular involvement.

CTA and MRA can be used to determine the degree of vessel wall involvement, demonstrating lesions related to TA, including a tortuous aorta with alternating segments of stenosis and dilation or occlusion, as well as involvement of aortic branches, particularly the carotid, left subclavian, and mesenteric arteries.

Vascular ultrasound is useful for detecting involvement of aortic branches, such as the subclavian arteries and common carotid arteries, while allowing evaluation of the carotid branches, vertebral arteries, and abdominal branches.
Vascular ultrasound can be used to monitor disease progression and staging, as well as therapeutic response.

sec.title: 5. Applications of multimodal cardiac imaging in storage diseases
5.1. Iron Overload Cardiomyopathy
sec.p: The term iron overload cardiomyopathy was introduced to describe cardiomyopathy resulting from iron accumulation in the myocardium, primarily due to genetically-determined iron metabolism disorders or multiple transfusions.324 In addition to being a major cause of morbidity, iron overload cardiomyopathy is responsible for one-third of deaths in hereditary hemochromatosis and is a leading cause of death in other conditions associated with secondary iron overload.325,326 Iron overload can be primary or secondary (Table 16).

caption.title: Main conditions that lead to iron overload

thead.style: border-top: thin solid; border-bottom: thin solid; border-color: #000000

tr.td: ➢ Type I: related to the HFE gene

list-item.p: Subtype A: related to the HJV gene
Subtype B: related to the HAMP gene

tr.td: ➢ Type III: Related to the TfR2 gene

sec.p: The primary form of iron overload is called hereditary hemochromatosis, an autosomal recessive genetic disease resulting from mutations in the genes that encode proteins involved in iron metabolism, causing increased iron absorption by the intestinal epithelium and further disruption of its metabolism, which leads to iron accumulation and consequent damage to various organs.327,328

Secondary iron overload is generally caused by high parenteral iron administration. It is mainly observed in association with hereditary or acquired anemias dependent on repetitive blood transfusions, which saturate the cells of the reticuloendothelial system with iron, subsequently spreading to other parenchymal cells (Table 16).329

Iron deposition occurs initially in the ventricular myocardium, followed by the atrial myocardium. It also affects the conduction system, especially the atrioventricular node, but to a lesser degree than the functional myocardium.329 It should be noted that myocardial iron overload, although a triggering factor in the development of iron overload cardiomyopathy, is not the only mechanism involved. Iron overload cardiomyopathy is a specific type of cardiomyopathy with a complex pathophysiology involving additional immunoinflammatory and genetic factors that affect pathogenesis. Two phenotypes of iron overload cardiomyopathy have been identified:325

list-item.p: Dilated phenotype: characterized by LV remodeling and leading to chamber dilation and reduced LVEF;
Restrictive phenotype: characterized by diastolic LV dysfunction with restrictive filling, preserved LVEF, pulmonary hypertension, and subsequent RV dilation.

sec.p: These phenotypes are followed by several other manifestations, including conduction system abnormalities, tachyarrhythmias, and perimyocarditis. If the cause of iron overload persists and no adequate iron chelation therapy is initiated, LV remodeling occurs in most patients with iron overload cardiomyopathy, in advanced stages leads to LV dilation and reduced LVEF (dilated phenotype).325,330

Approximately 10% of cases are characterized by severe iron overload and mild LV dysfunction, particularly in advanced stages, PH, RV dilation, and right HF without LV remodeling and with preserved LVEF, even in the final stages (restrictive phenotype).330–332

Iron overload cardiomyopathy, which presents distinct clinical characteristics and requires a specific diagnostic and therapeutic approach, should be considered in any patient with HF of unknown etiology. Patients may be asymptomatic in the early stages of the disease, although once HF develops, rapid deterioration follows.

In the initial assessment patients with iron overload, echocardiography is the main modality used to screen for heart disease, although its findings are nonspecific.325 Abnormalities in ventricular systolic and diastolic function, as well as pericardial and valvular involvement, can be detected. In early stages, slight dilation of the cardiac chambers and a minimal reduction in LVEF may be evident. In these patients, analysis of LV GLS can help confirm incipient myocardial dysfunction (Figure 20).

caption.title: Echocardiographic images of a 25-year-old patient with hereditary hemochromatosis. Left ventricular volumes and ejection fraction assessed by Simpson's method in 2-dimensional echocardiography (A) and 3-dimensional echocardiography (B and C) showing systolic function at the lower limit of normal and slight ventricular dilation. There is a slight reduction in left ventricular global longitudinal strain (-17.1%) and global circumferential strain (-24.2%) (D and E). LVEF: left ventricular ejection fraction; GCS: global circumferential strain; GLS: global longitudinal strain; RV: right ventricle; EDV: left ventricular end-diastolic volume; LV: left ventricle; ESV: left ventricular end-systolic volume.

sec.p: High cardiac output with chamber dilation, eccentric LVH, and normal or increased LVEF may also be observed.333 It should be noted that diastolic LV dysfunction and reduced LVEF can be masked by an anemia-induced high output state in patients with hemoglobinopathies and other hematological conditions. Thus, a pseudonormal pattern can often be found in transmitral flow,325 which can be exposed by refining the diastolic function analysis through investigation of pulmonary vein flow patterns or mitral annulus movement in tissue Doppler imaging.

Although sophisticated imaging methods, such as LV GLS, may be more sensitive markers of subclinical LV dysfunction, their results have been controversial in populations with hemochromatosis.334,335 prospective studies are needed to better evaluate subclinical LV dysfunction in individuals with chronically-treated hereditary hemochromatosis.

Although echocardiography can identify the consequences of iron overload on myocardial structure and function, it cannot accurately predict myocardial iron levels. Nevertheless, it is a simple method for screening asymptomatic patients and monitoring patients with known pathologies.325

CMR with T2* relaxometry is shortened in the presence of iron due to the metal's paramagnetic effect. T2* values < 20 ms indicate clinically relevant overload, and values < 10 ms are associated with a high risk of cardiac dysfunction and serious arrhythmias.336,337 There is a strong correlation between T2* values and iron concentration measured in biopsies, validating CMR as a reliable method for noninvasive assessment.338,339 The entire ventricle can also be mapped with the technique, avoiding sampling errors that can occur during biopsy.

Another promising tool is T1 mapping. In established cardiac iron overload, T1 and T2* are concordant. In CSF, native T1 values are reduced. However, in the 20–30 ms T2* range, T1 mapping appears to detect iron earlier.340–342
In advanced cases, LE can identify areas of myocardial fibrosis, which are associated with worse prognosis.340–342

In advanced cases, myocardial late enhancement can identify areas of myocardial fibrosis, which are associated with a worse prognosis.343 Although fibrosis is not a common finding in primary hemochromatosis, its presence in patients with secondary iron overload (such as thalassemias) may indicate more advanced disease.

Another significant advantage of CMR is its ability to monitor treatment response. Therapies such as phlebotomy or iron chelation (with desferrioxamine, deferasirox, or deferiprone) can reduce myocardial iron load, which can be monitored serially through CMR. Longitudinal thalassemia studies have shown that post-therapy improvement in T2* values is associated with cardiac function recovery and fewer adverse events.331,344 The main CMR changes in patients with hemochromatosis are described in Table 17.

caption.title: Main changes in hemochromatosis assessed by CMR

thead.style: border-top: thin solid; border-bottom: thin solid; border-color: #000000

fn.p: CMR: cardiac magnetic resonance imaging; ECV: extracellular volume; LVH: left ventricular hypertrophy; N/A: not applicable.

sec.p: LV dysfunction and PH can lead to impaired RV function.325 More recently, CMR data analysis in patients with thalassemia major showed that RVEF progressively decreased with increasing myocardial iron load, following a similar pattern to LVEF.345

Finally, it should be noted that serum ferritin levels do not correlate with myocardial iron overload severity, ie, high myocardial iron deposition can occur despite low serum ferritin levels.346 Therefore, diagnosis of iron overload cardiomyopathy is based on evidence of heart disease, particularly when LV diastolic dysfunction324,347 with restrictive LV filling or remodeling with chamber dilation and reduced LVEF co-occurs with iron overload (serum ferritin 300 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 55%) and cardiac siderosis (cardiac T2* < 20 ms), as outlined in Figure 21.

caption.title: Diagnosis flowchart for iron overload cardiomyopathy. Diagnosis requires: (1) iron overload (serum ferritin > 300 ng/mL, transferrin saturation > 55%); (2) cardiac siderosis (T2* < 20 ms); and (3) evidence of heart disease. LV: left ventricle; LVEF: LV ejection fraction; RV: right ventricle. Adapted from Kremastinos & Farmakis.331

sec.p: Table 18 presents practical recommendations (following the GRADE system) on echocardiography in patients with known or suspected iron overload cardiomyopathy.

sec.title: 5.2. Fabry Disease
sec.p: Anderson-Fabry disease (FD), a rare condition resulting from pathogenic variants in the GLA gene, leads to a deficiency of α-galactosidase, an enzyme responsible for the metabolism of glycosphingolipids (GL-3 and lyso-Gb3) in lysosomes. This results in the formation of cellular deposits that can be observed as early as intrauterine life. These deposits cause an intense inflammatory process and oxidative stress, evolving to cellular apoptosis and multisystem organ failure.348

Clinical manifestations depend on the genotype, since certain pathogenic variants determine the classic phenotype and others cause the alternate (late onset) phenotype. In the first subgroup, enzymatic activity < 5% determines very early symptoms in children as young as 2 years of age. Notable symptoms include the appearance of angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis, gastrointestinal disorders, corneal changes (verticillata), painful crises due to peripheral neuropathy, and proteinuria of varying intensity. Supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias, exercise intolerance, and mild valve insufficiency may occur in these early stages. These alterations tend to worsen in adolescence in cases not treated with specific therapy, whether enzyme replacement or oral chaperone therapy. In adulthood, significant changes may occur in the renal system (renal failure), cardiac system (marked increase in myocardial thickness, arrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, and a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy pattern with HFpEF), and central nervous system (cerebrovascular disease), with rapid progression to advanced disease and the need for replacement therapies such as dialysis.349,350

However, due to the presence of residual levels of enzymatic activity, symptoms in the alternate phenotype manifest later, generally in adulthood, and are more restricted to organs such as the heart and kidney. Nevertheless, this rules out neither cardiomyopathy nor nephropathy, and the potential for progression is as severe as in the classic form. Thus, the cardiac and renal changes are the same as in the classic form.349,350

Definitive diagnosis is based on identifying the pathogenic variant associated with α-galactosidase activity, along with the presence of clinical manifestations, typical histological changes, elevated levels of specific biomarkers (Gb3 and lyso-Gb3), and a family history of the disease.351

The complexity of the disease's clinical presentation reinforces the need for multidisciplinary research, including medical geneticists and specialists such as cardiologists, neurologists, and nephrologists, among others. Therapy that integrates nursing care, nutrition, and psychology is also important for optimizing follow-up and improving quality of life.352

Cardiologists must play a leading role in this, since cardiovascular and renal manifestations are the main causes of FD morbidity and mortality in Brazil. Clinical complaints and abnormalities on complementary cardiological examinations can determine the stage of disease progression and provide diagnostic and prognostic information that indicates the need for specific treatment.353

Electrocardiography should be performed for the initial evaluation of cardiac involvement in FD and should be repeated annually. The most frequent electrocardiographic findings are a short PR interval, signs of LV overload, and a corrected QT interval < 440 ms.354 Echocardiography is fundamental, especially in asymptomatic individuals or in cases with nonspecific symptoms. Furthermore, its low cost and availability allow heart disease progression to be assessed in the index patient, as well as phenotypic diagnosis of potentially affected family members. The main cardiac imaging findings are described in Table 19, Figure 22 and Figure 23.

B) Apical 4-chamber view showing the endocardial binary signal (myocardial birefringence aspect) in the inferior septal wall. sec.p: Increased LV and/or RV thickness (30%-40% of cases), usually in a concentric pattern and associated with preserved EF and diastolic function abnormalities, should raise suspicion of FD. The incidence of these changes increases with age, and the prevalence is similar in men and women.354,355

The use of 3D imaging techniques increases the accuracy of cardiac mass without the need for geometric inferences. In young individuals, abnormal diastolic function that is unexplained by coexisting diseases is usually the earliest echocardiographic manifestation of the disease and precedes hypertrophy. LVEF usually remains preserved throughout the natural course of the disease, and worsening systolic function is associated with the appearance of fibrosis and/or alterations such as renal dysfunction. The presence of endocardial binary sign shows a histological correlation with endocardial Gb3 deposits. These deposits can also affect valve tissue, causing mild valvular regurgitation. Ectasia of the initial portion of the thoracic aorta may occur, which generally does not evolve into aneurysmal forms with the potential for dissection.

GLS analysis aids in differential diagnosis from phenocopies and can identify segmental contractility changes in the basal segment of the inferolateral wall that may go unnoticed in conventional echocardiographic evaluation (Figure 22). Segmental strain dysfunction may indicate fibrotic changes, which are markers of chronic disease and poor cardiovascular prognosis. RV free wall strain may be reduced, even when other systolic function markers, such as TAPSE and S-wave velocity, are normal.356–358

In addition to characterizing myocardial tissue and providing prognostic information, CMR can be useful in treatment response assessment. CMR allows precise quantification of ventricular mass and can detect specific patterns of myocardial involvement that aid in differential diagnosis from phenocopies.359–362 One of the most significant contributions of CMR to FD management is the ability to detect and quantify myocardial fibrosis through LE. The characteristic LE pattern occurs predominantly in the basal inferolateral LV segments, typically mesocardial or subepicardial, which contrasts with the transmural enhancement pattern observed in ischemic cardiomyopathy or the diffuse subendocardial pattern seen in amyloidosis. This peculiar distribution of fibrosis reflects the underlying pathophysiological process of the disease, which results from the accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells.362 The presence and extent of LE have important prognostic value, correlating with the risk of ventricular arrhythmias and adverse cardiac events.362

Native T1 mapping has become another valuable tool in CMR assessment. Due to intracellular accumulation of sphingolipids, native T1 values are reduced in FD, which contrasts with the increase observed in most other cardiomyopathies (Table 20). Special care should be taken regarding T1 pseudonormalization in areas affected by LE. This finding is particularly useful in the differential diagnosis between other causes of LVH, being considered a marker of the disease. T2 mapping may show slightly increased overall values (Figure 23).348

caption.title: Recommendations on multimodal imaging for the diagnosis of Anderson-Fabry disease

thead.style: border-top: thin solid; border-bottom: thin solid; border-color: #000000

tr.td: TTE should be performed as a first-line imaging method in FD diagnosis and should be repeated annually or if new cardiac symptoms appear.355,356

Altered GLS, characterized by decreased myocardial strain in the basal segment of the inferolateral wall, is characteristic of FD and serves as a differential diagnosis for other diseases with a similar phenotype.355,356
When first-degree relatives are diagnosed and genetic testing is not possible, echocardiography should be used for family screening.355,357
CMR is the gold standard for cardiac investigation because it allows for better characterization of myocardial damage, provides prognostic information, and can assess treatment response.358–360
99mTc-sestamibi SPECT/CT can provide additional information about microcirculation.360

fn.p: 99mTc-PYP: 99m-technetium; FD: Anderson-Fabry disease; CMR: cardiac magnetic resonance imaging; CT: computed tomography; GLS: global longitudinal strain; SPECT: single-photon emission computed tomography; TTE: transthoracic echocardiogram.

sec.p: CMR also plays a crucial role in assessing the response to enzyme replacement therapy or molecular chaperone therapy. Longitudinal studies have demonstrated that effective treatment can lead to stabilization or even regression of ventricular hypertrophy, as well as prevent the progression of myocardial fibrosis.362 CMR allows for objective and reproducible monitoring of these changes, providing quantitative parameters that aid in therapeutic decision-making. T1 mapping has proven especially sensitive to changes in myocardial globotriaosylceramide content during treatment and may serve as an early biomarker of treatment response. In addition to morphological assessment and tissue characterization, CMR provides valuable information about cardiac function and prognosis356,362 (Table 20).

Although its diagnostic and prognostic role is still under investigation, SPECT/CT can also provide information about microcirculation through the radiotracer 99mTc-sestamibi. Complaints of ischemic chest pain associated with electrocardiographic changes and typical biomarkers are frequent in the absence of macrovascular coronary obstruction. Coronary flow reserve can also be assessed in these cases by CT or CMR.360,361
Table 20 presents the main recommendations on multimodal cardiac imaging assessment in FD according to the GRADE system.

The recommended frequency of cardiac imaging examinations in patients with FD is based on expert consensus and practices from reference centers. A publication from the University of Washington recommends annual echocardiography in men from 18 years of age and every 2 years in women aged 18 to 35 years; after 35 years of age, the frequency may be adjusted according to the clinical scenario.350

Multicenter studies and reviews suggest that, in clinical practice, echocardiography (including myocardial strain) should be performed every 6 to 12 months, especially in higher-risk or symptomatic patients, and may be performed earlier in cases of clinical worsening.363 Cardiac magnetic resonance is recommended every 1 to 2 years, depending on availability and disease stage.335,362,363

Thus, the frequency of imaging examinations should be individualized according to disease severity, symptoms, response to treatment, and availability of imaging modalities, with intensified follow-up in cases of higher risk or progression of cardiac involvement.363,364

caption.title: Key messages

list-item.p: The most typical echocardiographic findings in FD are increased myocardial thickness of the ventricular wall and papillary muscle, with preserved systolic function, diastolic dysfunction, binary endocardial appearance, and mild valvular regurgitation.
Reduced GLS in the basal segment of the inferolateral wall is characteristic of FD and helps differentiate it from other diseases of a similar phenotype.

CMR is useful for distinguishing ventricular hypertrophy in FD from that of other cardiomyopathies due to the symmetrical concentric thickening pattern, fibrosis in inferolateral basal segments, and typically reduced native T1 values in the septum.
Through CMR, the effects of enzyme replacement therapy or molecular chaperone therapy for FD can be assessed, including monitoring for hypertrophy regression and LE stabilization.

sec.title: 5.3. Glycogen Storage Diseases
sec.p: Glycogen storage diseases (GSD) are a heterogeneous group of genetic metabolic diseases caused by mutations in the genes that encode enzymes involved in glucose metabolism, leading to intracellular glycogen accumulation in various organs. There are more than 12 types of GSD, and here we highlight those that affect the heart and skeletal muscle: Pompe disease (GSD type IIa) (autosomal recessive with pathogenic variants in the gene encoding α-glucosidase acid),365 Danon disease (GSD type IIb) (X-linked inheritance and mutations in the LAMP2 gene, which encodes lysosome-associated membrane protein-2),366 and PRKAG2 syndrome (autosomal dominant with mutations in the PRKAG2 adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase gamma-2 regulatory subunit).367

GSD present different cardiac phenotypes, ranging from asymptomatic conditions to sudden cardiac death. Despite their broad range of clinical presentations, these diseases predominantly manifest in children (as early as the first year of life in Pompe disease) or young adults and have early increased LV wall thickness in common.

Echocardiography, the first-line imaging method, can reveal a hypertrophic, restrictive, or dilated phenotype.366,368,369 Hypertrophy is often severe (> 30 mm), biventricular, and rapidly progressive, especially in male Danon disease patients366 (Figure 24). Female Danon disease patients present with asymmetrical LVH, RVH, or, in 30% to 50% of cases, dilated or non-dilated hypokinetic phenotypes with slower progression. Dynamic obstruction of the LV outflow tract may also occur in GSD, especially Danon disease (up to 25% of the cases),366 and should be actively investigated in patients with dyspnea.

caption.title: Transthoracic echocardiogram images of a patient with PRKAG2 syndrome. Significant concentric left ventricular hypertrophy is observed in the parasternal longitudinal view (A) and the apical longitudinal view (B), in addition to significant right ventricular hypertrophy in the apical view (right chambers) (C). Polar map of a patient with moderate left ventricular systolic function impairment demonstrating reduced global longitudinal strain (-5.9%) and a striped appearance.

sec.p: Despite the crucial role of echocardiography, the clinical context is fundamental for the differential diagnosis with other hypertrophic phenocopies, especially sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, helping to guide the indication for genetic testing and/or biopsy.368 Electrocardiographic changes, such as a short PR interval, ventricular pre-excitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome), atrial fibrillation, intraventricular conduction delays, and sinoatrial or atrioventricular blocks, which require early pacemaker implantation, are considered warning signs of GSD.366 Unlike infiltrative cardiomyopathies, QRS voltage is normal or increased, which aids in the differential diagnosis with amyloidosis. Multisystem involvement (mainly myopathies and neurocognitive changes), LV diastolic dysfunction, and cardiopathy are the classic triad of Danon disease, which occurs more rarely in other GSD.366 The ventricular hypertrophy pattern can be identified by CMR, as discussed below.

Although advanced echocardiographic techniques, including speckle tracking and 3D myocardial strain imaging, are recommended in other hypertrophic or restrictive phenotypes,5,105 they lack robust validation in GSD. Reduced GLS with an apical sparing pattern (similar to that of CA) has been described in small retrospective case series on Danon disease, in which it was associated with worse outcomes.370,371

In 18 of 30 patients with PRKAG2 syndrome, Pena et al. observed a peculiar regional striped pattern (varying from light to dark pink) in the polar GLS map (Figure 24).372 In the same series, these authors found that RV function, assessed by GLS and 3D echocardiography, was below normal in more than half of the patients, showing a significant positive correlation between the RV free wall longitudinal strain and RVEF. These parameters have greater sensitivity in detecting myocardial dysfunction than traditional echocardiographic indices, such as TAPSE.373 In another study by the same group that included 7 children of parents with PRKAG2 syndrome, the echocardiographic findings indicated a trend towards cardiac hypertrophy.374
Table 21 summarizes the main echocardiographic characteristics of the GSD described above.

caption.title: Main echocardiographic characteristics of glycogen storage diseases

tr.td: Rapidly progressive biventricular hypertrophy, with a severe phenotype in men or a variable phenotype in women, ranging from hypertrophy to dilation and systolic dysfunction. LV outflow tract obstruction occurs in 25% of patients and should be actively investigated in patients with dyspnea. Strain may present with an apical sparing polar map pattern, similar to amyloidosis.
Concentric hypertrophy will rapidly progress to severe diffuse hypokinesia if left untreated. LV outflow tract obstruction may occur.

LV hypertrophy occurs in varying degrees, generally with a concentric pattern; RV hypertrophy is not uncommon; LV outflow tract obstruction is infrequent. In polar maps, strain may appear with a striped pattern.

fn.p: LV: left ventricle; right ventricle.

sec.p: The prognosis for hypertrophic phenocopies associated with GSD is generally worse than that of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy caused by variants of the sarcomeric protein gene. Of these, specific enzyme replacement therapy exists only for Pompe disease.365 However, early diagnosis facilitates therapy for HF and arrhythmias. Nevertheless, the benefits of enzyme replacement therapy in Pompe disease remain uncertain. Considering the severity and rapid progression of GSD, as well as its therapeutic implications, it is reasonable to recommend, even without robust evidence, echocardiography for disease screening every 1-2 years in symptomatic or asymptomatic children and adolescents with pathogenic variants and/or children of family members with early onset of GSD signs and symptoms. In individuals without the above described conditions, echocardiography is recommended every 3 to 5 years.366

CMR allows the detection of characteristic myocardial changes that can distinguish GSD from other forms of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, enabling early diagnosis and monitoring of disease progression.374 This is particularly valuable considering the rapid progression of some of these diseases (such as Danon disease and infantile Pompe disease) and the need for early intervention. LE patterns, native T1 mapping, and ECV calculation aid in differential diagnosis with other hypertrophic phenotypes, as well as in determining disease stage (Table 22). In Danon disease, the extent of LE correlates with the degree of cardiac dysfunction and has important prognostic value, being a risk marker for malignant ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. LE frequently presents a transmural or subepicardial distribution and involves multiple ventricular segments. CMR also allows for more accurate quantification of ventricular mass and wall thickness, as well as the detection of intracavitary thrombi secondary to ventricular dysfunction, overcoming some limitations of echocardiography, particularly the difficulty of visualizing cardiac segments, such as the apical region, the lateral wall, and the RV. Studies have shown that hypertrophy progresses more rapidly in LV diastolic dysfunction than in other cardiomyopathies, and CMR provides a sensitive method for monitoring it. The main CMR findings in patients with GSD are shown in Table 23.

sec.p: In the context of family counseling and carrier screening, CMR is a sensitive tool for detecting cardiac involvement in at-risk relatives, even in the absence of clinical symptoms. Considering the X-linked inheritance pattern, early identification of cardiac abnormalities in heterozygous women is particularly important, as they may develop cardiac manifestations later than men, but with equal severity.

The expert panel of this position statement recommends transthoracic echocardiography for clinical follow-up of patients diagnosed with GSD and for screening of cardiac involvement every 1 to 2 years in symptomatic or asymptomatic children and adolescents with pathogenic variants and/or offspring of family members with early onset of signs and symptoms of GSDs. Cardiac magnetic resonance may be performed every 1 or 2 years in symptomatic patients, in the presence of echocardiographic abnormalities, and in those with risk factors such as arrhythmias, HF, and clinical complications.184,375

caption.title: Key messages

list-item.p: GSD typically manifest in early life as LVH or biventricular hypertrophy in echocardiography.

For echocardiograms showing LVH or biventricular hypertrophy, the clinical context is crucial for differential diagnosis, especially age of onset, mode of inheritance, association with ventricular pre-excitation, and multisystem involvement.

Advanced echocardiography techniques, such as GLS and 3D, are promising for early detection of LV or biventricular dysfunction in patients with suspected or known GSD. The strain pattern in polar mapping can aid in the differential diagnosis with hypertrophic phenocopies
CMR helps distinguish GSD from other cardiomyopathies through LVH distribution, native T1 and ECV values associated with dilation, and early loss of ventricular systolic function.

sec.title: 6. Applications of Multimodal Cardiac Imaging in Neuromuscular Diseases
sec.p: Neuromuscular diseases are a heterogeneous group of rare degenerative conditions that affect motor, respiratory, and even swallowing function. The main conditions, Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD), and Friedreich ataxia (FA), are of genetic origin. DMD and BMD are X-linked genetic conditions, characterized by differing degrees of changes in dystrophin. Impairment may include cardiac function, which is a significant cause of mortality in these patients. There is no clear temporal correlation between skeletal muscle and myocardial involvement in any of these conditions, which represents a major challenge for cardiac dysfunction screening. Myocardial function assessment through noninvasive imaging methods, including their capabilities and recommendations, will be discussed below.

sec.title: 6.1. Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
sec.p: DMD is the most severe dystrophinopathy, leading to progressive motor function impairment, generally resulting in wheelchair dependence before 12 years of age.376 Although common, cardiomyopathy usually develops later in the course of the disease, with a dilated pattern that evolves to reduced LVEF around 14 years of age.377 About 33% of patients will develop dilated cardiomyopathy by 14 years of age, 50% between 14 and 18 years of age, and likely 100% by 18 years of age.378 Although there is still a scarcity of clinical studies with robust evidence, early diagnosis of cardiac involvement may allow for early cardioprotective therapy (with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or beta-blockers).378 A retrospective study found that, in < 4 years of follow-up, administering cardioprotective agents led to stabilized or even improved myocardial function in a significant percentage of the 69 patients.379

Due to its low cost and ease of access, TTE is the preferred method for evaluating and monitoring patients with DMD. Assessment is recommended at the time of diagnosis or beginning at 6 years of age, with evaluations every 2 years until 10 years of age, at which point annual evaluation is recommended.380,381 Myocardial involvement may begin regionally, primarily in the LV inferolateral wall (Figure 25). Advanced echocardiographic techniques for assessing ventricular function, such as multi-axis speckle-tracking strain analysis, including GLS and global circumferential strain parameters, has proven sensitive for early diagnosis of myocardial involvement.382,383 Initial studies point to the efficacy of regional strain as a means of identifying impaired myocardial strain in the LV inferolateral region.384

caption.title: Bulls-eye image and curves for each myocardial segment in apical projections of longitudinal myocardial strain measurement in a patient with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, showing reduced strain in the posterolateral segments despite preserved left ventricular segmental contractility.

sec.p: Studies comparing CMR with TTE in patients with DMD have shown that 20% to 40% of patients are underdiagnosed by TTE when using LVEF criteria.385,386 Reports of insufficient acoustic windows are also frequent in this patient population.387 In a recent cohort of 38 patients with DMD, Prakash et al. found that 52.6% had LVEF < 55% according to CMR and only 12% had abnormal GLS.388 A 2018 position statement recommended using TTE until around 6 to 7 years of age in patients with DMD and, as soon as possible, CMR for early detection of heart disease.389 It is important to consider that CMR is a more expensive and less readily available method, often requiring sedation in children or those with positioning difficulties, which can be common in this population.

sec.title: 6.2. Becker Muscular Dystrophy
sec.p: Unlike DMD, which is the more severe form, BMD has slower progression and generally milder symptoms.377 Histopathological studies have shown that cardiac damage can precede clinical symptoms, beginning as early as adolescence, even in asymptomatic individuals or those with little motor impairment.390 As in DMD, myocardial involvement generally includes the inferolateral LV wall (Figures 26 and 27). Cardiological follow-up should begin during childhood or adolescence, with periodic evaluations even in asymptomatic individuals (an annual frequency is suggested). Detecting early functional changes that indicate a need for therapeutic intervention is still a clinical challenge, although echocardiography is playing an increasingly important role.

caption.title: Echocardiographic images of a patient diagnosed with Becker muscular dystrophy, showing slight left ventricle dilation in the parasternal longitudinal view and little variation between diastolic (A) and systolic (B) diameters, with moderate systolic dysfunction. During systole, there is no thickening of the inferolateral wall (B). Image provided by Dr. Viviane Hotta.

Cardiac magnetic resonance images of a patient with Becker muscular dystrophy showing left ventricular dilation with significant left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Thinning of the basal and middle segments of the inferior and inferolateral walls is observed (A to F). Extensive heterogeneous late enhancement is observed in the basal and middle segments of the anterior lateral and mediobasal inferolateral walls (C, E, and F), with an appearance usually found in muscular dystrophy.

sec.p: Although cardiac function analysis should be based on LVEF quantification, there is also evidence that advanced techniques, such as speckle-tracking myocardial strain assessment, allow for early diagnosis of global or regional myocardial dysfunction. An observational study391 found that 77.5% of patients with BMD presented with abnormal GLS (≥ −18%), while only 60% had reduced LVEF. Notably, GLS was altered in 17.5%, despite normal LVEF. After 2 years of follow-up, GLS had deteriorated significantly, while LVEF remained stable, demonstrating the role of strain analysis as an early and sensitive marker of disease progression. GLS was also significantly correlated with troponin I and NT-proBNP levels, but not with muscle or respiratory function. Tissue Doppler and LA function assessment, although less explored in BMD, can provide additional information on early diastolic dysfunction, especially when associated with atrial strain analysis. Early recognition of these changes is essential for disease-modifying therapies, such as cardioprotective agents, which can affect disease progression, morbidity, and mortality.

CMR is the diagnostic tool of choice for evaluating cardiac abnormalities like myocardial edema and fibrosis. Different techniques, such as T1 and T2 sequencing, LE, and multiparametric mapping are fundamental for assessing these patients, as is contractile function assessment and LVEF and RVEF calculation. Recent studies have found that LE increases with age (from 17% at < 10 years of age to 59% in those > 15 years of age with reduced LVEF).392 There is a linear correlation between the presence and number of segments affected by fibrosis and LVEF decrease. Typically, the fibrosis pattern in DMD and BMD affects the subepicardium or mesocardium, progressing with disease progression to transmural fibrosis, most frequently in the inferolateral LV wall.393 Recent studies have suggested that adipose tissue infiltration into skeletal muscle plays an important role in myocardial disease progression, and myocardial LE may result from the combination of fibrosis and adipose tissue.394 Thus, CMR plays a fundamental role not only in assessing the presence of fibrosis and ventricular function, but also in evaluating progression at a cellular level through the transformation of adipose tissue in heart muscle.

sec.title: 6.3. Friedreich Ataxia
sec.p: Friedreich Ataxia (FA), a neurodegenerative disease with an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, is caused by repeat expansion in the FXN gene, resulting in frataxin protein deficiency. Clinically, it is characterized by progressive ataxia, cerebellar dysfunction, scoliosis, DM and, often, cardiomyopathy, which is one of the most severe and lethal manifestations of the disease.376,395

FA-associated cardiomyopathy is characterized by LVH, primarily septal, which can progress to fibrosis, ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmias, and HF, the latter being the leading cause of death among patients. Although the relationship between atrial fibrillation-associated cardiomyopathy and neurological degeneration is unclear, regular assessment of cardiac involvement is essential in clinical practice. FA-associated cardiomyopathy can be classified into 4 categories based on interventricular septum thickness in diastole and LVEF, as shown in Table 24. However, with disease progression, LV mass may reduce due to LVH regression and increased myocardial fibrosis. These parameters can be assessed by serial 2D echocardiography. LVEF estimation is crucial, since decreased values are associated with a higher risk of mortality.396

Moderate LVH, possible onset of remodeling.
Ventricular dilation, decreased myocardial GLS, possible signs of fibrosis.

fn.p: AInterventricular septum thickness in diastole considered normal based on Henry et al.'s normogram.397 CMP-FA: Friedreich ataxia-associated cardiomyopathy; GLS: global longitudinal strain; IVSd: interventricular septum thickness in diastole; LVEF: left ventricular ejection fraction; LVH: left ventricular hypertrophy.

sec.p: Advanced echocardiographic techniques like LV GLS analysis can indicate early changes in relation to LVEF and are useful for detecting subclinical dysfunction. The most common alteration is diastolic dysfunction (84%), which is mainly pseudonormalized and can be determined through the transmitral E/A ratio, mitral flow deceleration rate, and the E/e’ ratio.398

Given the scarcity of controlled clinical trials and systematic reviews focused on diagnosing FA-associated cardiomyopathy, we suggest a systematic evaluation of the TTE parameters listed in Table 25.

caption.title: Key echocardiographic parameters for cardiac evaluation of Friedreich ataxia

thead.style: border-top: thin solid; border-bottom: thin solid; border-color: #000000

fn.p: IVSd: interventricular septum thickness in diastole; LV: left ventricular; LVEF: LV ejection fraction.

sec.p: CMR, a valuable tool for characterizing fibrosis and myocardial remodeling in patients with FA, even in the absence of clinical HF, can detect LVH and myocardial fibrosis.399 CMR can also reveal early myocardial remodeling, characterized by hypertrophy and increased ECV, even in patients with preserved LVEF.399 The technique also allows detection of abnormalities in myocardial perfusion reserve, which are indicative of myocardial ischemia in the absence of epicardial CAD.400

Thus, in light of evidence in the literature, for patients with suspected cardiomyopathy related to neuromuscular diseases (mainly DMD, BMD, and FA), we recommend a cardiomyopathy screening strategy involving TTE, taking accessibility and cost into consideration. According to GRADE criteria,401 this recommendation is strong, based on moderate-certainty evidence (mainly for DMD) regarding early diagnosis, which could beneficially affect the progression of myocardial dysfunction (although the level of certainty about its impact on survival is still low) (Table 26).

caption.title: Recommendations on echocardiography in patients with neuromuscular degenerative diseases

thead.style: border-top: thin solid; border-bottom: thin solid; border-color: #000000

tr.td: Transthoracic echocardiography should be performed as a first-line assessment in patients with neuromuscular diseases to screen for ventricular dysfunction.

sec.p: In patients with DNM, evaluation is recommended at the time of diagnosis or from 6 years of age, with assessments every 2 years until 10 years of age, when annual evaluation is recommended. In patients with evidence of reduced LVEF or in the presence of abnormalities detected by GLS, annual evaluation is recommended.380,381

sec.title: 7. Perspectives
sec.p: In cardiology, as in all medical specialties, multimodal integration of imaging techniques is a clear necessity for patients. Each cardiac imaging method has its advantages and disadvantages, and no single method can provide all of the required information about the complex functioning of the cardiovascular system.

Given the particularities and the interface between inflammatory factors and traditional cardiovascular risk factors in each specific disease, recommendations for the indication and frequency of each cardiac imaging examination should be individualized for each disease and patient. The purpose of these examinations is to reduce the risk of cardiometabolic and inflammatory complications related to traditional risk factors and to facilitate early diagnosis of abnormalities, including HF (with preserved or reduced EF), as well as coronary, valvular, myocardial, pericardial, and aortic diseases associated with systemic diseases. Thus, given the complexity and cardiac complications of each disease, a structured multimodal approach for the diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of these abnormalities is critically necessary.4,9–11,402,403

Despite the well-established value of new technologies for the early detection of subclinical changes in cardiac function, echocardiographic myocardial strain analysis is not yet routinely used. Because this method depends on specific equipment, examiner training, and requires more time to perform, it demands adequate remuneration, thus limiting its use in clinical practice. Nevertheless, in clinical practice, myocardial strain assessment should be systematically integrated into conventional echocardiographic analysis.5,6 New cardiac CT-associated techniques for investigating myocardial ischemia, such as fractional flow reserve and perfusion assessment, can improve diagnostic accuracy, but they remain underutilized.9,10,403 However, 4D CMR allows for 3D visualization of vascular flow over time and quantitative measurement of transvalvular and intracavitary flow.11,403

Additionally, the integration of precision medicine and artificial intelligence in cardiovascular practice has transformed the assessment and management of systemic diseases with cardiac involvement.404,405 Precision medicine is an effort to tailor diagnosis and treatment based on the specific biological, clinical, and imaging characteristics of each patient. Artificial intelligence enhances this approach by processing large volumes of data, identifying subtle patterns and predicting disease trajectories with greater accuracy. When applied to multimodal cardiac imaging, artificial intelligence can integrate data on functional, structural, and tissue characterization, promoting more precise phenotypic stratification and aiding in the early detection of myocardial involvement.406,407

In systemic diseases, early and accurate characterization of cardiac changes is crucial for risk stratification and treatment planning. In diseases such as amyloidosis or sarcoidosis, for example, combining CMR and PET or SPECT increases diagnostic sensitivity and can identify subclinical myocardial inflammation or infiltration. Similarly, in autoimmune rheumatic diseases, integrating echocardiography, nuclear medicine, and CMR can reveal early signs of ischemia, myocarditis, and fibrosis, which often go unnoticed in the early stages.

Thus, the convergence of precision medicine, artificial intelligence, and multimodal cardiac imaging fosters a deeper understanding of the cardiovascular impact of systemic diseases, enabling screening and early diagnosis of cardiovascular complications in patients with generalized systemic diseases, as well as personalized monitoring of cardiac function and associated changes during follow-up.

caption.title: Key messages

list-item.p: Impaired cardiac function, a significant cause of mortality, may occur in neuromuscular diseases such as DMD, BMD, and FA.
DMD is the most severe form of dystrophinopathy. Although common, cardiomyopathy (with a dilated pattern) usually develops later, evolving to reduced LVEF at around 14 years of age.
TTE is the preferred method for assessing and monitoring patients with neuromuscular diseases.
In DMD and BMD, the pattern of myocardial involvement can begin regionally, primarily in the LV inferolateral wall.
LV GLS has proven to be a sensitive parameter for early diagnosis of myocardial involvement in neuromuscular diseases.
FA-associated cardiomyopathy is characterized by LVH, primarily septal, which can progress to fibrosis, ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmias, and HF.

Patients with FA and advanced heart disease may experience LVH regression and increased myocardial fibrosis. LVEF analysis with TTE is crucial, since reduced values are associated with a higher mortality risk.

sec.title: 8. Conclusions
sec.p: Due to the wide variety of cardiovascular manifestations in systemic diseases, routine requests for multimodal cardiac imaging in clinical follow-up must be standardized. However, no routine for requesting cardiac imaging examinations has been established. Advances in cardiac imaging techniques, the growing evidence of their usefulness in patients with systemic diseases, and multidisciplinary work among cardiologists, rheumatologists, pulmonologists, neurologists, etc. will contribute to the development of a standardized routine for multimodal imaging in these patients.
